lessons.title: Physical Quantities and Estimation
lessons.notes_html:
A physical quantity is anything that can be measured: length, mass, time, temperature, force and so on. Every measurement of a physical quantity is written as a number together with a unit, for example 3.51 m.

Estimation means finding the approximate value (the order of magnitude) of a quantity without an exact measurement, using known reference values and simple reasoning. Estimates are rounded to one significant figure and are useful for checking whether a calculated result is reasonable.

Estimating the Base Quantities

  • Length is estimated by comparing with a metre rule or with the known height of a person.
  • Mass is estimated by comparing with standard masses we handle daily, such as a 1 kg packet.
  • Time is estimated by counting a regular event, such as a pendulum swing or a heartbeat.

Worked Example: Your Age in Seconds

A pupil of age 17 years: convert this age into seconds.

Step 1: 17 years x 365 = 6205 days.

Step 2: 6205 days x 24 = 148,920 hours.

Step 3: 148,920 x 3600 = 536,112,000 s.

Answer: about 5.36 x 108 s (leap years add roughly one extra day per four years).

Worked Example: Distance Covered by Light in One Year

Light travels at 3 x 108 m s-1. How far does it travel in one year? This distance is called one light year.

Step 1: Time in one year = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 3.15 x 107 s.

Step 2: Distance = speed x time = 3 x 108 x 3.15 x 107.

Answer: about 9.5 x 1015 m. A light year is a unit of distance, not of time.

lessons.title: Base Units and Derived Units
lessons.notes_html:
Base units are the units of the seven fundamental (base) physical quantities of the SI system. They are independent of one another. All other units are derived units, obtained by multiplying or dividing base units.

Base QuantityUnitSymbol
Lengthmetrem
Masskilogramkg
Timeseconds
Electric currentampereA
TemperaturekelvinK
Amount of substancemolemol
Luminous intensitycandelacd

Derived Units in Base Units

  • Speed = distance / time, so its unit is m s-1.
  • Force = mass x acceleration = kg x m s-2, called the newton (N).
  • Energy = force x distance = kg m2 s-2, called the joule (J).
  • Power = work / time = kg m2 s-3, called the watt (W).

Derived units may carry special names like newton, joule and watt, but every one of them can be written in base units.

Quantities with No Units

Some quantities are pure ratios, so their units cancel and they have no unit and no dimensions:

  • Strain = change in length / original length
  • Refractive index = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in the medium
  • Relative density = density of a substance / density of water

lessons.title: Dimensions of Physical Quantities
lessons.notes_html:
The dimensions of a physical quantity show how it is built from the base quantities. We write mass as [M], length as [L] and time as [T], with powers showing how many times each base quantity appears.

QuantityRelationDimensions
Velocitydisplacement / time[L T-1]
Accelerationvelocity / time[L T-2]
Forcemass x acceleration[M L T-2]
Work and energyforce x distance[M L2 T-2]
Moment of inertiamass x (length)2[M L2]
Strainlength / lengthdimensionless
  • Quantities with the same dimensions are of the same kind: work, kinetic energy and potential energy all have dimensions [M L2 T-2] and the same unit, the joule.
  • A quantity whose dimensions contain no M, L or T is dimensionless, like strain.
  • Dimensions tell us the nature of a quantity even when we do not know its unit.

Worked Example: Dimensions of the Spring Constant

By Hooke's law, F = k x. Find the dimensions of the spring constant k.

Step 1: k = F / x, so k has the dimensions of force divided by length.

Step 2: Dimensions of force = [M L T-2]; dividing by [L] gives [M T-2].

Answer: k has dimensions [M T-2] and unit N m-1.

mcqs.why: Moment of inertia = mass x (length)2, so its dimensions are [M] x [L2] = [M L2], with no time dimension.

lessons.title: Dimensional Analysis: Homogeneity of Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The principle of homogeneity says that in any correct physical equation, every term that is added, subtracted or equated must have exactly the same dimensions. An equation that fails this test is certainly wrong.

Worked Example: Checking an Equation of Motion

Check whether S = vi t + (1/2) a t2 is dimensionally correct.

Step 1: Left side: S is a length, dimensions [L].

Step 2: First term: vi t has dimensions [L T-1] x [T] = [L].

Step 3: Second term: a t2 has dimensions [L T-2] x [T2] = [L]. The factor 1/2 is a pure number and has no dimensions.

Answer: all terms have dimensions [L], so the equation is homogeneous and dimensionally correct.

Limits of Dimensional Analysis

  • It cannot find pure numbers in a formula, such as 1/2 or 2π.
  • It cannot distinguish between different quantities that share the same dimensions, such as work and torque.
  • An equation can be dimensionally correct and still be physically wrong, but it can never be correct if it is dimensionally wrong.

mcqs.why: Homogeneity requires every added, subtracted or equated term to have exactly the same dimensions; an equation failing this test is certainly wrong.

lessons.title: Dimensional Analysis: Deriving Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
Dimensional analysis can also derive a formula. We assume the unknown quantity depends on certain variables raised to unknown powers, equate the dimensions on both sides, and solve for the powers.

Worked Example: Formula for Centripetal Force

The centripetal force Fc on a particle depends on its mass m, velocity v and the radius r of the circle. Derive the formula.

Step 1: Suppose Fc = ma vb rc. Writing dimensions: [M L T-2] = [M]a [L T-1]b [L]c.

Step 2: Compare powers of M: a = 1. Powers of T: -b = -2, so b = 2.

Step 3: Powers of L: b + c = 1, so c = 1 - 2 = -1.

Answer: Fc = m v2 / r (any pure number in the true formula cannot be found this way).

Worked Example: Dimensions of the Gravitational Constant

From F = G m1 m2 / r2, find the dimensions of G.

Step 1: G = F r2 / (m1 m2).

Step 2: Dimensions = [M L T-2] [L2] / [M2] = [M-1 L3 T-2].

Answer: G has dimensions [M-1 L3 T-2].

lessons.title: Accuracy and Precision
lessons.notes_html:
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another. Accuracy is the closeness of a measurement to the true value.

  • Four darts landing together but far from the centre are precise but not accurate.
  • Four darts clustered on the centre are both precise and accurate.
  • An accurate measurement is the more reliable one: repeated readings may all agree with each other yet all be wrong together, for example with a wrongly zeroed instrument.

Precision depends on the least count of the instrument: the smaller the least count, the finer the readings. Of the common length instruments, the screw gauge gives the most precise measurement, then vernier calipers, then the metre rule and tape.

Using an instrument of smaller least count decreases the limit of precision: the fractional uncertainty falls, so the result lies closer to the true value and the accuracy increases.

lessons.title: Uncertainties in Measurements
lessons.notes_html:
Every measurement contains some uncertainty, because every instrument has a smallest division it can read (its least count) and because conditions and readings can never be perfect. No measurement is ever exact.

Types of Uncertainty

Absolute uncertainty is the uncertainty written in the same unit as the measurement, for example 3.51 m ± 0.01 m.

Fractional uncertainty = absolute uncertainty / measured value

Percentage uncertainty = fractional uncertainty x 100

Worked Example: Percentage Uncertainty

The length of a body is measured as 3.51 m with an absolute uncertainty of 0.01 m. Find the percentage uncertainty.

Step 1: Fractional uncertainty = 0.01 / 3.51 = 0.0028.

Step 2: Percentage uncertainty = 0.0028 x 100.

Answer: 0.28 %

Reducing Uncertainty

  • Repeat the measurement several times and take the mean value; averaging cancels random errors.
  • Use an instrument with a smaller least count.
  • Remove zero error and avoid parallax error by careful technique.
  • Keep the experimental conditions steady.

When quantities are multiplied or divided, their percentage uncertainties are added to give the uncertainty in the result; when quantities are added or subtracted, their absolute uncertainties are added.

Key Points

  • Estimation gives the order of magnitude of a quantity and checks whether a result is reasonable.
  • There are seven SI base units; all derived units are built from them.
  • Strain, refractive index and relative density have no units and no dimensions.
  • Dimensions are written with [M], [L] and [T]; equal dimensions mean quantities of the same kind.
  • A correct equation must be homogeneous: all its terms have the same dimensions.
  • Dimensional analysis can derive formulae but cannot find pure numbers like 1/2 or 2π.
  • Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.
  • Every measurement has uncertainty; percentage uncertainties add when quantities multiply or divide.

lessons.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
lessons.notes_html:
Scalar quantities have magnitude only: mass, time, temperature, energy, work and speed. Vector quantities have magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum.

Representing a Vector

  • Graphically, a vector is drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead: the length of the line (to a chosen scale) gives the magnitude and the arrowhead gives the direction.
  • In writing, a vector is shown in bold (A) or with an arrow above it.
  • In unit-vector form: A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k, where i, j and k are unit vectors along the x, y and z axes.

Rules of Vector Algebra

  • A scalar can never be added to or subtracted from a vector: the two are different kinds of quantity, and the result could have neither a pure magnitude nor a single direction. Only like quantities can be added: scalar with scalar, vector with vector.
  • A vector cannot be divided by another vector, because a vector has no unique inverse; the quotient would not be well defined.
  • A vector can be multiplied by a scalar: this changes its magnitude but keeps its direction (a negative scalar also reverses the direction).

lessons.notes_html:
A vector can be resolved into two perpendicular (rectangular) components. If vector A makes an angle θ with the x-axis, drop perpendiculars from its tip onto the two axes; the two projections are the components.

Ax = A cos θ

Ay = A sin θ

  • Ax — component along the x-axis
  • Ay — component along the y-axis
  • θ — angle of the vector with the x-axis

The original vector is recovered from its components:

A = √(Ax2 + Ay2)

θ = tan-1 (Ay / Ax)

  • The vertical component is maximum when θ = 90°, because sin 90° = 1.
  • The two components are equal when cos θ = sin θ, that is at θ = 45°; then each component is A / √2.
  • When both components are negative, the vector lies in the third quadrant.

Worked Example: Direction of a Vector

Find the angle that the vector A = 2 i + 2 j makes with the x-axis.

Step 1: Ax = 2 and Ay = 2.

Step 2: tan θ = Ay / Ax = 2 / 2 = 1.

Answer: θ = 45 degrees.

mcqs.why: Dropping perpendiculars from the tip of A onto the axes gives the rectangular components Ax = A cos theta and Ay = A sin theta.

mcqs.why: The component along the y-axis is the projection Ay = A sin theta, while the x-component is A cos theta.

mcqs.why: The original vector is recovered from its components: A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2), by Pythagoras on the rectangle of components.

mcqs.q: The direction of a vector is found from its components by
mcqs.why: The angle with the x-axis satisfies tan theta = Ay / Ax, so theta = tan^-1 (Ay / Ax).

180 degrees, because the vector is longest
mcqs.why: Ay = A sin theta, and sin theta is largest at theta = 90 degrees where sin 90 = 1, so the vertical component is maximum then.

options: 45 degrees, each component then being A / sqrt(2)
mcqs.why: The components are equal when cos theta = sin theta, that is at theta = 45 degrees; then each component is A / sqrt(2).

mcqs.why: Negative Ax points in the -x direction and negative Ay in the -y direction, which together place the vector in the third quadrant.

mcqs.why: Ay = A sin theta = 10 x sin 60 = 10 x 0.866 = 8.66. The x-component is 10 x cos 60 = 5.

lessons.title: Resultant of Two Vectors
lessons.notes_html:
The resultant of two vectors is the single vector that has the same effect as the two vectors acting together. For two vectors A and B with angle θ between them:

R = √(A2 + B2 + 2AB cos θ)

  • R — magnitude of the resultant
  • θ — angle between A and B when placed tail to tail
  • For perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°), cos θ = 0 and the formula becomes R = √(A2 + B2).
  • For parallel vectors (θ = 0°), R = A + B, the maximum possible resultant.
  • For anti-parallel vectors (θ = 180°), R = A - B, the minimum possible resultant.

Worked Example: Resultant of Two Forces

Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at 90 degrees to each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant force.

Step 1: R = √(A2 + B2) = √(32 + 42).

Step 2: R = √(9 + 16) = √25.

Answer: R = 5 N.

mcqs.q: The resultant of two vectors A and B with angle theta between them has magnitude
options: R = A + B for every angle
mcqs.why: The resultant formula is R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta), where theta is the angle between A and B placed tail to tail.

mcqs.q: For two perpendicular vectors (theta = 90 degrees), the resultant is
mcqs.why: At theta = 90 degrees, cos theta = 0, so the 2AB cos theta term vanishes and R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2).

mcqs.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at 90 degrees to each other. Their resultant is
mcqs.why: R = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N, the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: The resultant of two vectors is maximum when the angle between them is
mcqs.why: For parallel vectors (theta = 0), cos theta = 1 and R = A + B, the maximum possible resultant.

mcqs.q: The resultant of two vectors is minimum when the angle between them is
mcqs.why: For anti-parallel vectors (theta = 180 degrees), cos theta = -1 and R = A - B, the minimum possible resultant.

mcqs.q: The resultant of two vectors is defined as
options: the sum of the magnitudes of the two vectors in all cases
the vector sum only when the vectors are parallel
the single vector that has the same effect as the two vectors acting together
the difference of the two vectors
mcqs.why: The resultant is the single vector that has the same effect as the two vectors acting together; its magnitude depends on the angle between them.

mcqs.why: The notes specify that theta is the angle between A and B when placed tail to tail.

mcqs.q: Two perpendicular vectors have magnitudes 6 and 8. Their resultant is
mcqs.why: For perpendicular vectors R = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10.

mcqs.q: Two vectors of 5 units each act in the same direction. Their resultant is
mcqs.why: Same direction means theta = 0, so R = A + B = 5 + 5 = 10 units, the maximum resultant for these vectors.

mcqs.q: Two vectors of 5 units each act in opposite directions. Their resultant is
mcqs.why: Opposite directions means theta = 180 degrees, so R = A - B = 5 - 5 = 0 units, the minimum resultant.

lessons.title: Scalar (Dot) Product
lessons.notes_html:
The scalar product (dot product) of two vectors is a scalar quantity:

A . B = AB cos θ

  • A, B — magnitudes of the two vectors
  • θ — the smaller angle between them

Properties of the Dot Product

  • It is commutative: A . B = B . A, because AB cos θ is the same in either order.
  • It is distributive over addition: A . (B + C) = A . B + A . C.
  • It is zero for perpendicular vectors, since cos 90° = 0, and maximum (equal to AB) for parallel vectors.
  • It can be negative: when θ is between 90° and 180°, cos θ is negative. Example: the work done by friction is negative, because friction acts opposite to the displacement (θ = 180°).
  • A vector dotted with itself gives the square of its magnitude: A . A = A2.
  • For unit vectors: i . i = j . j = k . k = 1, and i . j = j . k = k . i = 0.
  • In components: A . B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz.

Work done is the most familiar dot product: W = F . S. The projection of A on B is (A . B) / B.

Worked Example: Projection of One Vector on Another

Find the projection of A = 2 i + 4 j on B = 4 i + 3 k.

Step 1: A . B = (2)(4) + (4)(0) + (0)(3) = 8.

Step 2: Magnitude of B = √(42 + 32) = √25 = 5.

Step 3: Projection = (A . B) / B = 8 / 5.

Answer: 8/5 units.

Worked Example: Work Done by a Force

A force F = 4 i - 3 j + 2 k N displaces an object from A(3, 2, -1) to B(2, -1, 4). Find the work done.

Step 1: Displacement S = B - A = (2 - 3) i + (-1 - 2) j + (4 + 1) k = -i - 3 j + 5 k m.

Step 2: W = F . S = (4)(-1) + (-3)(-3) + (2)(5) = -4 + 9 + 10.

Answer: W = 15 J. (Note: the book prints 32 J for this question, which does not follow from the printed data; the step-by-step dot product gives 15 J.)

mcqs.why: When theta is between 90 and 180 degrees, cos theta is negative, so A . B is negative; the work done by friction is the standard example.

mcqs.why: Friction acts opposite to the displacement (theta = 180 degrees, cos theta = -1), so its dot product with displacement, the work, is negative.

mcqs.why: With theta = 0 between a vector and itself, A . A = A A cos 0 = A^2, the square of its magnitude.

mcqs.why: A . B = (2)(4) + (4)(0) + (0)(3) = 8. Magnitude of B = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5. Projection = (A . B) / B = 8 / 5 units.

mcqs.why: W = F . S = (4)(-1) + (-3)(-3) + (2)(5) = -4 + 9 + 10 = 15 J. (The book prints 32 J, which does not follow from the printed data.)

lessons.title: Vector (Cross) Product
lessons.notes_html:
The vector product (cross product) of two vectors is itself a vector:

A x B = AB sin θ n

  • n — unit vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B
  • θ — the smaller angle between A and B

Direction: The Right-Hand Rule

Point the fingers of the right hand along A and curl them towards B; the extended thumb points along A x B. Equivalently, A x B points in the direction a right-handed screw advances when turned from A to B.

Properties of the Cross Product

  • It is anti-commutative: A x B = - (B x A).
  • It is distributive over addition.
  • It is zero for parallel or anti-parallel vectors, since sin 0° = sin 180° = 0, and maximum (equal to AB) for perpendicular vectors.
  • A x A = 0 for every vector.
  • Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by A and B.
  • For unit vectors: i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j; reversing the order reverses the sign.
  • Torque and angular momentum are cross products: τ = r x F and L = r x p.

Worked Example: Angle Between Two Vectors

The magnitudes of the dot and cross products of two vectors are 6 and 6√3 respectively. Find the angle between them.

Step 1: A . B = AB cos θ = 6 and |A x B| = AB sin θ = 6√3.

Step 2: Dividing, tan θ = (6√3) / 6 = √3.

Answer: θ = 60 degrees.

A useful identity links the two products: (A x B)2 + (A . B)2 = A2B2, because sin2 θ + cos2 θ = 1.

Key Points

  • Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
  • A vector is drawn as an arrow: length gives magnitude, arrowhead gives direction.
  • Components: Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ; the components are equal at θ = 45°.
  • Dot product A . B = AB cos θ is a scalar; it is zero for perpendicular vectors and can be negative.
  • Cross product A x B = AB sin θ n is a vector; its direction follows the right-hand rule.
  • The cross product is zero for parallel vectors and maximum for perpendicular vectors.
  • (A x B)2 + (A . B)2 = A2 B2.

mcqs.q: The vector (cross) product of two vectors is given by

A x B = AB sin theta, a scalar
A x B = AB tan theta n
A x B = AB sin theta n, a vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B
mcqs.why: The cross product A x B = AB sin theta n is itself a vector, where n is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B.

drawing it parallel to A + B

mcqs.why: The angle between a vector and itself is 0, and sin 0 = 0, so A x A = 0 for every vector.

the area of the parallelogram formed by A and B
the projection of A on B
mcqs.why: The notes state that the magnitude of the cross product equals the area of the parallelogram formed by A and B.

mcqs.why: i x j = k, j x k = i and k x i = j, following the cyclic order; reversing the order reverses the sign.

mcqs.q: Torque and angular momentum are both examples of
options: cross products: tau = r x F and L = r x p
mcqs.why: Torque tau = r x F and angular momentum L = r x p are cross products, so both are vectors perpendicular to the plane of their two factors.

mcqs.why: AB cos theta = 6 and AB sin theta = 6 sqrt(3). Dividing, tan theta = 6 sqrt(3) / 6 = sqrt(3), so theta = 60 degrees.

lessons.title: Equations of Motion
lessons.notes_html:
For motion in a straight line with uniform acceleration, three equations connect velocity, acceleration, time and displacement. They are derived from the definitions of velocity and acceleration.

vf = vi + a t

S = vi t + (1/2) a t2

vf2 = vi2 + 2 a S

  • vi — initial velocity, vf — final velocity
  • a — uniform acceleration, t — time, S — displacement

Derivation from the Velocity-Time Graph

  • The slope of the velocity-time line is the acceleration: a = (vf - vi) / t, which rearranges to the first equation.
  • The area under the line is the displacement: the rectangle vi t plus the triangle (1/2)(vf - vi) t, which gives the second equation.
  • Eliminating t between the first two equations gives the third equation.

Worked Example: A Braking Train

A train moves with a uniform velocity of 24 m s-1. The driver applies the brakes and the train comes to rest with uniform retardation in 12 s. Find the distance covered after the brakes are applied.

Step 1: vi = 24 m s-1, vf = 0, t = 12 s. Average velocity = (24 + 0) / 2 = 12 m s-1.

Step 2: S = average velocity x t = 12 x 12.

Answer: S = 144 m.

mcqs.why: The slope of the velocity-time line is a = (vf - vi) / t, the acceleration; the area under the line gives the displacement.

mcqs.why: The area under the velocity-time line is the rectangle vi t plus the triangle (1/2)(vf - vi) t, which equals the displacement S.

mcqs.why: Eliminating t between the first two equations gives vf^2 = vi^2 + 2 a S, which links velocities and displacement without time.

in a circle at constant speed
mcqs.why: The three equations connect velocity, acceleration, time and displacement for motion in a straight line with uniform (constant) acceleration.

lessons.title: Motion under Gravity
lessons.notes_html:
A body falling freely under gravity (air resistance neglected) has a constant acceleration g = 9.8 m s-2 vertically downwards. The equations of motion apply with a replaced by g; for a body dropped from rest, vi = 0.

vf = g t

h = (1/2) g t2

vf2 = 2 g h

  • h — height fallen
  • Air resistance opposes the fall, so in air a real body accelerates less than g and may reach a constant terminal velocity; in a vacuum all bodies fall with the same g.

Worked Example: A Coin Dropped from a Tower

A coin is dropped from a tower and reaches the ground after 5 s. Find (a) the height of the tower and (b) the speed with which the coin hits the ground.

Step 1: h = (1/2) g t2 = (1/2) x 9.8 x 52 = 4.9 x 25 = 122.5 m.

Step 2: vf = g t = 9.8 x 5 = 49 m s-1.

Answer: (a) 122.5 m (b) 49 m s-1.

mcqs.why: With vi = 0, S = vi t + (1/2) g t^2 reduces to h = (1/2) g t^2 for a body dropped from rest.

The coin in the previous question hits the ground at a speed of

mcqs.why: At terminal velocity the body falls at constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero; air resistance has grown to balance its weight.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws and Linear Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
The linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity:

p = m v

  • p — momentum (kg m s-1), a vector in the direction of v

Newton's second law in its general form states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the applied force: F = Δp / t. For a fixed mass this becomes the familiar F = m a.

Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum

In the absence of an external force, the total momentum of a system of interacting bodies remains constant: the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after it.

m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2

A rocket works on Newton's third law: it throws exhaust gases backwards at high speed, and the gases push the rocket forwards with an equal and opposite force.

Worked Example: A Truck Couples to a Car

A 4000 kg truck moving at 20 m s-1 strikes a stationary 800 kg car and couples to it. Find their combined speed after impact.

Step 1: Total momentum before = 4000 x 20 + 800 x 0 = 80,000 kg m s-1.

Step 2: Total mass after coupling = 4000 + 800 = 4800 kg.

Step 3: Combined speed = 80,000 / 4800 = 16.7 m s-1.

Answer: 16.7 m s-1.

lessons.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions in One Dimension
lessons.notes_html:
In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, and the bodies separate with no loss of energy. In an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not: part of it changes into heat, sound or deformation. If the bodies stick together, the collision is perfectly inelastic.

Final Velocities in an Elastic Collision

For masses m1 and m2 with initial velocities u1 and u2:

v1 = ((m1 - m2)u1 + 2m2u2) / (m1 + m2)

v2 = ((m2 - m1)u2 + 2m1u1) / (m1 + m2)

Special Cases

  • Equal masses, one at rest: the moving body stops and the other moves off with its velocity — the velocities are exchanged.
  • Light body hits a heavy body at rest: the light body rebounds with nearly its own speed.
  • Heavy body hits a light body at rest: the light body is carried forward at nearly twice the heavy body's speed.
  • Perfectly inelastic: the bodies move together with V = (m1u1 + m2u2) / (m1 + m2).

Worked Example: Two Spheres Collide

Two spheres of masses m and 2m move to the right with velocities 4 m s-1 and 2 m s-1. They collide elastically. Find their final velocities.

Step 1: v1 = ((m - 2m)(4) + 2(2m)(2)) / (3m) = (-4m + 8m) / 3m = 1.33 m s-1.

Step 2: v2 = ((2m - m)(2) + 2(m)(4)) / (3m) = (2m + 8m) / 3m = 3.33 m s-1.

Answer: 1.33 m s-1 and 3.33 m s-1, both to the right. (Note: the book prints 4 m s-1 for the second sphere, which does not conserve momentum; the values above conserve both momentum and kinetic energy.)

mcqs.q: In an elastic collision, the quantities conserved are
mcqs.why: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved and the bodies separate with no loss of energy.

mcqs.q: In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is not conserved because part of it changes into
mcqs.why: In an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but part of the kinetic energy changes into heat, sound or deformation.

mcqs.q: A collision in which the bodies stick together is called
mcqs.why: If the bodies stick together, the collision is perfectly inelastic, and they move with the common velocity V = (m1 u1 + m2 u2) / (m1 + m2).

mcqs.q: When two equal masses collide elastically with one at rest,
options: the moving body stops and the other moves off with its velocity
both move off at half the velocity
the moving body rebounds at the same speed
mcqs.why: For equal masses in an elastic collision the velocities are exchanged: the moving body stops and the stationary one takes its velocity.

mcqs.q: When a light body hits a heavy stationary body elastically, the light body
options: rebounds with nearly its own speed
carries the heavy body forward at twice its speed
mcqs.why: A light body hitting a heavy body at rest rebounds with nearly its own speed; the heavy body barely moves.

mcqs.q: When a heavy body hits a light stationary body elastically, the light body is carried forward at
options: nearly twice the heavy body's speed
mcqs.why: A heavy body hitting a light body at rest sends the light body forward at nearly twice the heavy body's speed, while the heavy body continues almost unchanged.

mcqs.q: Spheres of mass m and 2m move at 4 m s-1 and 2 m s-1 and collide elastically. The sphere of mass m ends with velocity
In the same collision, the sphere of mass 2m ends with velocity
mcqs.why: v2 = ((2m - m)(2) + 2(m)(4)) / (3m) = (2m + 8m) / 3m = 10/3 = 3.33 m s-1. (The book prints 4 m s-1, which does not conserve momentum.)

mcqs.q: For a perfectly inelastic collision, the common velocity is
mcqs.why: Conservation of momentum with the bodies moving together gives (m1 + m2) V = m1 u1 + m2 u2, so V = (m1 u1 + m2 u2) / (m1 + m2).

mcqs.q: Two bodies of 1 kg and 3 kg move towards each other at 4 m s-1 and 2 m s-1 (taking the 1 kg body's direction as positive) and stick together. Their common velocity is
mcqs.why: V = (m1 u1 + m2 u2) / (m1 + m2) = (1 x 4 + 3 x (-2)) / 4 = (4 - 6) / 4 = -0.5 m s-1, i.e. 0.5 m s-1 in the 3 kg body's original direction.

lessons.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
lessons.notes_html:
When bodies collide in a plane, they generally scatter in different directions. The collision is handled by resolving all momenta along two perpendicular axes.

  • Momentum is conserved separately along each axis: total momentum along x before = total momentum along x after, and the same for y.
  • In an elastic two-dimensional collision, kinetic energy is also conserved.
  • In an inelastic two-dimensional collision, kinetic energy is partly lost as heat, sound or deformation, but momentum is still conserved along each axis.
  • If the bodies stick together, they move off as one body whose velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass, in the direction of the total momentum vector.

mcqs.q: In a two-dimensional collision, momentum is conserved
options: only if the bodies stick together
separately along each of two perpendicular axes
only in the direction of the faster body
mcqs.why: The collision is handled by resolving all momenta along two perpendicular axes: momentum along x is conserved and momentum along y is conserved separately.

mcqs.q: In an elastic two-dimensional collision, in addition to momentum,
options: the scattering angle is always 90 degrees
mcqs.why: In an elastic two-dimensional collision, kinetic energy is also conserved, just as in one dimension.

mcqs.q: In an inelastic two-dimensional collision, kinetic energy is partly lost as heat, sound or deformation, but
options: momentum is still conserved along each axis
mcqs.why: Even when KE is partly lost, momentum is still conserved along each axis in an inelastic two-dimensional collision.

mcqs.q: If two bodies stick together in a two-dimensional collision, the combined body moves with velocity equal to
options: the sum of the two velocities
the total momentum divided by the total mass, in the direction of the total momentum vector
the total mass divided by the total momentum
the velocity of the heavier body
mcqs.why: Stuck together, they move off as one body whose velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass, in the direction of the total momentum vector.

mcqs.q: Bodies colliding in a plane generally
mcqs.why: When bodies collide in a plane, they generally scatter in different directions, which is why momenta must be resolved along two axes.

mcqs.q: The method used to handle a two-dimensional collision is to
options: add the speeds of the bodies
resolve all momenta along two perpendicular axes and conserve each component
mcqs.why: Resolving along two perpendicular axes lets momentum conservation be applied separately to the x-components and the y-components.

mcqs.q: Two bodies of equal mass stick together after colliding at right angles with equal speeds v. The magnitude of the total momentum is proportional to
mcqs.why: The total momentum components are m v along each axis, so the magnitude is sqrt((m v)^2 + (m v)^2) = sqrt(2) m v, and the combined body moves in that direction.

mcqs.q: In a two-dimensional collision with no external force, the total momentum along the y-axis after the collision equals
options: the total momentum along the y-axis before the collision
the total momentum along the x-axis
mcqs.why: Momentum is conserved separately along each axis: total y-momentum before = total y-momentum after, and the same for x.

mcqs.q: A two-dimensional collision differs from a one-dimensional collision because the bodies move
options: in a plane and can scatter in different directions
mcqs.why: In a plane the bodies generally scatter in different directions, so the collision must be treated with momentum components along two perpendicular axes.

mcqs.q: If the total momentum before a two-dimensional sticking collision is P and the total mass is M, the speed of the combined body is
mcqs.why: The combined body moves with velocity = total momentum / total mass = P / M, in the direction of the total momentum vector.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion
lessons.notes_html:
A projectile is a body thrown into the air which then moves under gravity alone (air resistance neglected). Its motion is two-dimensional: a combination of uniform horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion.

  • The horizontal component of velocity stays constant: vx = vi cos θ, because there is no horizontal acceleration.
  • The vertical component changes under gravity: vy = vi sin θ - g t. It is zero at the highest point.
  • Horizontal displacement: x = vi cos θ x t. Vertical displacement: y = vi sin θ x t - (1/2) g t2.
  • The acceleration is g, vertically downwards, at every point of the path.
  • The speed is maximum at projection and at landing (equal to vi) and minimum at the highest point, where only vi cos θ remains.

mcqs.q: A projectile is a body thrown into the air which then moves under
options: gravity and a continuing push from the thrower
mcqs.why: A projectile moves under gravity alone; its motion combines uniform horizontal motion with accelerated vertical motion.

mcqs.q: The horizontal component of a projectile's velocity
options: stays constant at vi cos theta, because there is no horizontal acceleration
becomes zero at the highest point
mcqs.why: There is no horizontal acceleration, so vx = vi cos theta stays constant throughout the flight.

mcqs.q: The vertical component of velocity at the highest point of a projectile's path is
mcqs.why: vy = vi sin theta - g t decreases under gravity and is zero at the highest point; only the horizontal component remains there.

mcqs.q: Throughout a projectile's flight, its acceleration is
options: g, vertically downwards, at every point of the path
different at each point of the path
mcqs.why: The only acceleration is gravity: g vertically downwards at every point of the path, including the highest point.

mcqs.q: The speed of a projectile is minimum at
options: the highest point, where only vi cos theta remains
mcqs.why: At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so the speed is just vi cos theta, its minimum; it is maximum at projection and at landing.

mcqs.q: The speed of a projectile at landing (on the same level) is
options: equal to its projection speed vi
mcqs.why: The speed is maximum at projection and at landing (equal to vi) and minimum at the highest point.

mcqs.q: The horizontal displacement of a projectile after time t is
options: x = vi sin theta x t
x = vi cos theta x t
x = vi cos theta x t - (1/2) g t^2
mcqs.why: Horizontal motion is uniform, so x = vx t = vi cos theta x t; the vertical displacement is y = vi sin theta x t - (1/2) g t^2.

mcqs.q: The vertical displacement of a projectile after time t is
options: y = vi cos theta x t
y = vi sin theta x t + (1/2) g t^2 measured upward
y = vi sin theta x t - (1/2) g t^2
mcqs.why: Vertically the projectile accelerates downwards, so y = vi sin theta x t - (1/2) g t^2 with upward taken as positive.

mcqs.q: A ball is projected at 30 m s-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Its initial vertical component of velocity is
mcqs.why: vy initially = vi sin theta = 30 x sin 30 = 30 x 0.5 = 15 m s-1. The horizontal component is 30 x cos 30 = 26 m s-1.

mcqs.q: For the same ball, the horizontal component of velocity throughout the flight is
mcqs.why: vx = vi cos theta = 30 x cos 30 = 30 x 0.866 = 26 m s-1, and it stays constant because there is no horizontal acceleration.

lessons.title: Time of Flight, Maximum Height and Range
lessons.notes_html:
T = 2 vi sin θ / g

H = vi2 sin2 θ / (2 g)

R = vi2 sin 2θ / g

  • T — time of flight: the time from projection until the projectile returns to the same level
  • H — maximum height, reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero
  • R — horizontal range
  • θ — angle of projection with the horizontal
  • The range is maximum at θ = 45°, where sin 2θ = 1.
  • Complementary angles give the same range: θ and (90° - θ), for example 30° and 60°. The ranges at (45° + θ) and (45° - θ) are also equal.
  • The maximum height is greatest for vertical projection, θ = 90°.
  • Height and range are equal when θ is about 76°.

Worked Example: A Cricket Ball

A cricket ball is hit upward at 45 degrees with a velocity of 20 m s-1. Find (a) the maximum height, (b) the time of flight and (c) how far away it hits the ground. (Take g = 9.8 m s-2.)

Step 1: H = vi2 sin2 θ / (2 g) = (202 x 0.5) / (2 x 9.8) = 200 / 19.6 = 10.2 m.

Step 2: T = 2 vi sin θ / g = (2 x 20 x 0.707) / 9.8 = 28.3 / 9.8 = 2.9 s.

Step 3: R = vi2 sin 2θ / g = (400 x 1) / 9.8 = 41 m.

Answer: (a) 10.2 m (b) 2.9 s (c) 41 m.

mcqs.q: The time of flight of a projectile (returning to the same level) is
mcqs.why: T = 2 vi sin theta / g: the time from projection until the projectile returns to the same level.

mcqs.q: The maximum height of a projectile is
mcqs.why: H = vi^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g), reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero at the top of the path.

mcqs.q: The horizontal range of a projectile is
mcqs.why: R = vi^2 sin 2 theta / g; it is maximum at theta = 45 degrees where sin 2 theta = 1.

mcqs.q: The range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is
mcqs.why: R = vi^2 sin 2 theta / g is maximum when sin 2 theta = 1, i.e. 2 theta = 90 degrees, so theta = 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: Complementary angles of projection give the same range; an example pair is
mcqs.why: Angles theta and (90 - theta) give the same range because sin 2 theta is the same for both; 30 and 60 degrees are the standard example.

mcqs.q: The maximum height is greatest for a projection angle of
mcqs.why: H = vi^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g) is greatest when sin theta = 1, at theta = 90 degrees, vertical projection.

mcqs.q: Height and range of a projectile are equal when theta is about
mcqs.why: The notes state that height and range are equal when the projection angle is about 76 degrees.

mcqs.q: A cricket ball hit at 45 degrees with velocity 20 m s-1 reaches a maximum height of
The time of flight of the same cricket ball is
The range of the same cricket ball is
mcqs.why: R = vi^2 sin 2 theta / g = (400 x 1) / 9.8 = 41 m, since at 45 degrees sin 2 theta = sin 90 = 1.

lessons.title: Work Done by a Constant Force
lessons.notes_html:
Work is done when a force moves its point of application. For a constant force it is the scalar (dot) product of force and displacement:

W = F S cos θ

  • F — force, S — displacement, θ — angle between them
  • The unit of work is the joule (J): 1 J = 1 N x 1 m.

Positive, Negative and Zero Work

  • Positive work (θ less than 90°): the force has a component along the displacement, e.g. pushing a cart forward; the kinetic energy increases.
  • Negative work (θ greater than 90°): the force opposes the displacement, e.g. friction or a braking force; the kinetic energy decreases.
  • Zero work (θ = 90°): the force is perpendicular to the displacement, e.g. the centripetal force on a satellite; also zero when there is no displacement, e.g. pushing against a wall.
  • For a body moving with uniform velocity, the net force is zero, so the net work done is zero.

Worked Example: Cart Pushed Up an Incline

A 250 kg cart is pushed up an inclined surface until it is 3 m above the ground, friction neglected. How much work does the pushing force do?

Step 1: Against gravity, the work done equals the gain in potential energy: W = m g h.

Step 2: W = 250 x 9.8 x 3 = 7350 J.

Answer: 7350 J. (The answer does not depend on the slope of the incline, only on the vertical height gained.)

mcqs.q: The work done by a constant force is
options: W = F S cos theta, the scalar (dot) product of force and displacement
W = F S, whatever the angle
mcqs.why: Work is the dot product of force and displacement: W = F S cos theta, where theta is the angle between them; 1 J = 1 N x 1 m.

mcqs.q: The unit of work, the joule, is equal to
mcqs.why: The unit of work is the joule: 1 J = 1 N x 1 m, the work of a 1 N force moving its point of application 1 m along its line.

mcqs.q: Work is positive when the angle between force and displacement is
options: less than 90 degrees, so the force has a component along the displacement
mcqs.why: Positive work (theta less than 90 degrees): the force has a component along the displacement, e.g. pushing a cart forward, and KE increases.

mcqs.q: Work is negative when
options: the force opposes the displacement (theta greater than 90 degrees), as with friction or braking
the force is perpendicular to the displacement
the body moves at uniform velocity
mcqs.why: Negative work occurs when the force opposes the displacement, e.g. friction or a braking force; the kinetic energy decreases.

mcqs.q: The work done by the centripetal force on a satellite is zero because
options: the force is perpendicular to the displacement (theta = 90 degrees)
mcqs.why: Zero work occurs at theta = 90 degrees: the centripetal force is perpendicular to the displacement, so W = F S cos 90 = 0.

mcqs.q: Pushing against a wall that does not move does zero work because
mcqs.why: Work needs displacement of the point of application; pushing against an unmoving wall gives zero displacement and therefore zero work.

mcqs.q: A 250 kg cart is raised 3 m above the ground (friction neglected). The work done against gravity is
mcqs.why: W = m g h = 250 x 9.8 x 3 = 7350 J. It depends only on the vertical height gained, not on the slope of the incline.

mcqs.q: For a body moving with uniform velocity, the net work done is
options: zero, because the net force is zero
equal to F S cos theta of the largest force
mcqs.why: Uniform velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero and hence the net work done is zero.

mcqs.q: A force of 50 N pulls a box 4 m at 60 degrees to the direction of motion. The work done is
mcqs.why: W = F S cos theta = 50 x 4 x cos 60 = 200 x 0.5 = 100 J.

mcqs.q: When work is done against gravity, it equals
options: the loss in kinetic energy in all cases
the gain in potential energy, m g h
mcqs.why: Against gravity the work done equals the gain in potential energy W = m g h, independent of the path or slope taken.

lessons.title: Work Done by a Variable Force
lessons.notes_html:
Many forces change during the motion — for example the force of a spring grows as it is stretched. The work done by a variable force is the area under the force-displacement graph between the starting and finishing positions.

  • The graph is divided into narrow strips of width Δx; each strip has area F Δx, the work done over that small displacement.
  • Adding all the strips gives the total area under the curve, which is the total work.
  • For a spring, F = k x gives a triangular area: W = (1/2) k x2.

mcqs.q: The work done by a variable force is found from
options: the maximum force multiplied by the distance
the slope of the force-displacement graph
the area under the force-displacement graph between the starting and finishing positions
the average of the first and last forces only
mcqs.why: Many forces change during the motion; the work done by a variable force is the area under its force-displacement graph.

mcqs.q: On a force-displacement graph, a narrow strip of width delta x has area F delta x, which represents
options: the total work in all cases
the work done over that small displacement
mcqs.why: Each narrow strip has area F delta x, the work done over that small displacement; adding all the strips gives the total work.

mcqs.q: For a spring stretched by x, the work done (and elastic PE stored) is
mcqs.why: For a spring F = k x gives a triangular area under the F-x graph: W = (1/2) k x^2.

mcqs.q: The F-x graph for a spring obeying F = k x is triangular because
options: the force grows steadily (linearly) as the spring is stretched
the force decreases as it stretches
mcqs.why: The force of a spring grows as it is stretched, F = k x, so the graph is a rising straight line and the area beneath it is a triangle.

mcqs.q: A spring of k = 200 N m-1 is stretched by 0.1 m. The work done is
The total work of a variable force is found by
options: multiplying the final force by the total distance
reading the highest point of the curve
dividing the area by the distance
adding the areas of all the narrow strips under the curve
mcqs.why: Adding all the strips gives the total area under the curve, which is the total work done by the variable force.

mcqs.q: An example of a variable force is
options: the force of a spring, which grows as it is stretched
the weight of a body near the Earth
a constant push on a cart
the tension in a rigid rod at rest
mcqs.why: The notes give the spring force as the example: it changes during the motion, growing as the spring is stretched.

mcqs.q: Doubling the stretch of a spring multiplies the stored elastic energy by
options: four, because W = (1/2) k x^2 depends on x^2
mcqs.why: W = (1/2) k x^2: doubling x makes x^2 four times bigger, so the work and stored energy become four times as large.

mcqs.q: The work done by a variable force between two positions is measured between
options: the starting and finishing positions on the F-x graph
the origin and the peak of the curve only
mcqs.why: The work is the area under the force-displacement graph between the starting and finishing positions of the motion.

mcqs.q: If the F-x graph is a straight horizontal line (constant force F) up to displacement S, the area is F S, which equals
options: the momentum gained in all cases
the work done by the constant force
mcqs.why: For a constant force the area is the rectangle F x S, matching W = F S cos theta with theta = 0.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the ability of a body to do work. Its two mechanical forms are kinetic energy and potential energy.

KE = (1/2) m v2

PE = m g h

  • Kinetic energy is the energy due to motion. It can never be negative: mass is always positive and v2 is always positive, so KE is zero at rest and positive in motion.
  • If the speed is doubled, KE becomes four times; if tripled, nine times.
  • Gravitational potential energy is the energy due to height h above a chosen reference level. PE is always relative: a bucket at the bottom of a well has zero PE relative to the bottom, but negative PE (-m g h) relative to the ground surface. Only changes in PE matter physically.
  • Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring is (1/2) k x2.

Worked Example: Speed and Kinetic Energy of a Van

A force of 6000 N is applied horizontally on a van of mass 2500 kg, starting from rest. After travelling 110 m, find its speed and kinetic energy.

Step 1: Work done = F x S = 6000 x 110 = 660,000 J. By the work-energy theorem this equals the KE gained.

Step 2: KE = (1/2) m v2, so v2 = 2 x 660,000 / 2500 = 528, and v = 23 m s-1.

Answer: speed 23 m s-1, KE = 660 kJ.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is given by
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy, the energy due to motion, is KE = (1/2) m v^2; it is zero at rest and positive in motion.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy can never be negative because
options: mass is always positive and v^2 is always positive
it is measured from a reference level
mcqs.why: KE = (1/2) m v^2: mass is always positive and v^2 is always positive, so KE is zero at rest and positive in motion, never negative.

mcqs.q: If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
mcqs.why: KE depends on v^2: doubling the speed makes v^2 four times bigger, so KE becomes four times; tripling the speed makes it nine times.

mcqs.q: If the speed of a body is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes
mcqs.why: KE = (1/2) m v^2, so tripling v multiplies v^2, and hence KE, by 3^2 = 9.

mcqs.q: Gravitational potential energy is given by
options: PE = m h, independent of any reference
PE = m g h, measured from a chosen reference level
mcqs.why: PE = m g h is the energy due to height h above a chosen reference level; PE is always relative to that level.

mcqs.q: A bucket at the bottom of a well has PE relative to the ground surface that is
options: negative (-m g h), because it lies below the reference level
mcqs.why: PE is relative: zero at the bottom of the well by that choice, but -m g h relative to the ground surface; only changes in PE matter physically.

mcqs.q: The elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring is
mcqs.why: Elastic PE stored in a stretched spring is (1/2) k x^2, the same as the work done stretching it (the triangular area under the F-x graph).

mcqs.q: A force of 6000 N acts on a 2500 kg van over 110 m from rest. The kinetic energy gained is
mcqs.why: Work done = F x S = 6000 x 110 = 660,000 J, and by the work-energy theorem this equals the KE gained.

mcqs.q: The final speed of that van is
Energy is defined as
options: the ability of a body to do work
the product of mass and velocity
mcqs.why: Energy is the ability of a body to do work; its two mechanical forms are kinetic energy and potential energy.

lessons.title: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservative Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Work-Energy Theorem

The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy:

W = (1/2) m vf2 - (1/2) m vi2

  • If the net work is positive, the body speeds up; if negative, it slows down; if zero, its KE does not change.

Worked Example: Work Needed to Accelerate a Body

How much work is required to accelerate a body of mass 200 kg from 5 m s-1 to 15 m s-1? If it covers 150 m during this time, what is the net force on it?

Step 1: W = (1/2) m (vf2 - vi2) = (1/2) x 200 x (225 - 25) = 100 x 200 = 2 x 104 J.

Step 2: F = W / S = 20,000 / 150 = 133 N.

Answer: work 2 x 104 J, net force 133 N.

Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces

A conservative force has three properties:

  • The work done by it between two points is independent of the path taken.
  • The work done by it around any closed path is zero.
  • It can be linked to a potential energy, so mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved under it.

Gravitational and electrostatic forces are conservative. Friction is non-conservative: the work it does depends on the path, and mechanical energy is lost as heat.

Key Points

  • Equations of motion: vf = vi + a t; S = vi t + (1/2) a t2; vf2 = vi2 + 2 a S.
  • On a velocity-time graph, the slope is acceleration and the area is displacement.
  • Momentum p = m v; force equals the rate of change of momentum.
  • Total momentum is conserved when no external force acts.
  • Elastic collisions conserve momentum and KE; inelastic collisions conserve momentum only.
  • Projectile: horizontal velocity constant, vertical acceleration g; range is maximum at 45 degrees.
  • Work W = F S cos θ; the work of a variable force is the area under its F-x graph.
  • KE = (1/2) m v2 is always positive; PE = m g h is measured from a chosen reference level.
  • Net work equals the change in kinetic energy (work-energy theorem).
  • Friction is a non-conservative force; gravity is conservative.

mcqs.q: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals
options: the change in its kinetic energy: W = (1/2) m vf^2 - (1/2) m vi^2
the change in its potential energy in all cases
its momentum change divided by time
mcqs.why: The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, W = (1/2) m vf^2 - (1/2) m vi^2.

mcqs.q: If the net work done on a body is positive, the body
options: must be moving in a circle
mcqs.why: Positive net work increases KE so the body speeds up; negative net work slows it down; zero net work leaves its KE unchanged.

mcqs.q: The work required to accelerate a 200 kg body from 5 m s-1 to 15 m s-1 is
If that body covers 150 m while accelerating, the net force on it is
mcqs.why: F = W / S = 20,000 / 150 = 133 N, using the work found from the work-energy theorem.

mcqs.q: A conservative force is one for which the work done between two points
options: is independent of the path taken
cannot be linked to a potential energy
mcqs.why: A conservative force: work between two points is path-independent, work around a closed path is zero, and it can be linked to a potential energy.

mcqs.q: The work done by a conservative force around any closed path is
options: equal to the change in KE
mcqs.why: One of the three properties of a conservative force is that the work done around any closed path is zero.

mcqs.q: Under a conservative force alone, the quantity conserved is
mcqs.why: A conservative force can be linked to a potential energy, so mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved under it.

mcqs.q: Friction is a non-conservative force because
options: it does no work at all
it is too weak to matter
its work around a closed path is zero
the work it does depends on the path, and mechanical energy is lost as heat
mcqs.why: Friction is non-conservative: the work it does depends on the path taken, and mechanical energy is lost as heat.

mcqs.q: Gravitational and electrostatic forces are examples of
mcqs.why: The notes name gravitational and electrostatic forces as conservative; friction is the standard non-conservative example.

mcqs.q: If the net work done on a body is zero, its kinetic energy
mcqs.why: By the work-energy theorem W = change in KE, so zero net work means zero change in kinetic energy, even if individual forces do work.

lessons.title: Angular Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration
lessons.notes_html:
Angular displacement θ is the angle swept out by a line joining a moving particle to the centre of its circle. It is a vector, directed along the axis of rotation by the right-hand rule.

Three Units of Angle

  • The degree: one revolution = 360 degrees.
  • The radian: the angle subtended at the centre when the arc length equals the radius; one revolution = 2π radians. The radian is the SI unit.
  • The revolution: one complete turn.

So 85.95 degrees is 1.5 radians, since 57.3 degrees make one radian.

S = r θ

  • S — arc length, r — radius, θ — angular displacement in radians

Angular velocity ω is the rate of change of angular displacement, ω = Δθ / Δt, measured in rad s-1. Angular acceleration α is the rate of change of angular velocity, α = Δω / Δt, measured in rad s-2. A body moving with constant angular velocity has zero angular acceleration.

Worked Example: Angular Speed of the Earth

The Earth completes one rotation about its axis in 24 hours. Find (a) its angular speed and (b) the tangential speed of a body at the equator. (Radius of the Earth = 6.4 x 106 m.)

Step 1: ω = 2π / T = 2π / (24 x 3600) = 6.28 / 86,400 = 7.3 x 10-5 rad s-1.

Step 2: v = r ω = 6.4 x 106 x 7.3 x 10-5 = 467 m s-1.

Answer: (a) 7.3 x 10-5 rad s-1 (b) 467 m s-1.

mcqs.q: Angular displacement is measured in the SI unit
mcqs.why: Angles are measured in degrees, radians or revolutions; the radian is the SI unit. One revolution = 360 degrees = 2 pi radians.

mcqs.q: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre when
options: the arc length equals the diameter
the arc length equals the radius
mcqs.why: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre when the arc length equals the radius; one revolution = 2 pi radians.

mcqs.q: Arc length and angular displacement are related by
options: S = r theta, with theta in radians
mcqs.why: S = r theta, where S is arc length, r the radius and theta the angular displacement in radians.

mcqs.q: One radian is approximately equal to
mcqs.why: 57.3 degrees make one radian, so 85.95 degrees is 1.5 radians, as given in the notes.

lessons.title: Linear and Angular Variables
lessons.notes_html:
For circular motion the linear and angular quantities are linked because the radius r stays constant. Differentiating S = r θ with respect to time gives each relation in turn:

v = r ω

at = r α

ac = v2 / r = r ω2

  • v — tangential (linear) speed, directed along the tangent to the circle
  • at — tangential acceleration, present only when the speed changes
  • ac — centripetal acceleration, directed towards the centre; it exists whenever the direction of motion changes, even at constant speed
  • The angular velocity vector points along the axis of rotation, while the linear velocity points along the tangent — the two are always perpendicular.

Worked Example: A Geostationary Satellite

A geostationary satellite revolves around the Earth in an orbit of radius 4.24 x 107 m with a time period of 24 hours. Find (a) its tangential speed and (b) its centripetal acceleration.

Step 1: ω = 2π / T = 7.3 x 10-5 rad s-1 (the same as the Earth's spin, which is why the satellite stays fixed over one place).

Step 2: v = r ω = 4.24 x 107 x 7.3 x 10-5 = 3.08 x 103 m s-1.

Step 3: ac = r ω2 = 4.24 x 107 x (7.3 x 10-5)2 = 0.224 m s-2.

Answer: (a) 3.08 x 103 m s-1 (b) 0.224 m s-2.

lessons.title: Centripetal Acceleration and Centripetal Force
lessons.notes_html:
A body moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because the direction of its velocity changes continuously. This centripetal acceleration points towards the centre of the circle:

ac = v2 / r

The force that produces it is the centripetal force:

Fc = m v2 / r = m r ω2

  • Centripetal force is not a new kind of force: it is supplied by whatever real force acts towards the centre — gravitation for a satellite, tension for a whirling stone, friction for a turning car.
  • Because the centripetal force is always perpendicular to the displacement, it does no work: W = F S cos 90° = 0. For the same reason its torque about the centre is zero (r and F are anti-parallel), so it changes neither the speed nor the angular momentum of the body — only its direction.
  • A centrifuge uses this principle in reverse: rapid rotation throws denser material outward, separating substances of different densities.

Worked Example: Centripetal Force on a Particle

A particle of mass 100 g moves along a circular path of radius 10 cm with a velocity of 10 m s-1. Find the centripetal force.

Step 1: m = 0.1 kg, r = 0.1 m, v = 10 m s-1.

Step 2: Fc = m v2 / r = 0.1 x 102 / 0.1 = 0.1 x 100 / 0.1.

Answer: Fc = 100 N.

lessons.title: Moment of Inertia
lessons.notes_html:
Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass: it measures the resistance of a body to a change in its rotational motion. For a single particle, I = m r2; for a whole body, I is the sum of m r2 over all its particles.

I = Σ m r2

BodyAxisMoment of Inertia
Hoop or thin ringthrough centreM R2
Disc or solid cylinderthrough centre(1/2) M R2
Solid spherethrough centre(2/5) M R2
Thin rodthrough centre(1/12) M L2
  • Moment of inertia grows with the mass and with the square of the size: mass far from the axis counts most.
  • Lead is much denser than copper, so a lead sphere of the same mass has a smaller radius and therefore a smaller I = (2/5) M R2: it is easier to rotate.
  • Of two cylinders of the same mass, the one with the larger radius has the larger moment of inertia and needs a larger torque (τ = I α) to start rotating.
  • The Earth is denser at its core, so its moment of inertia is about 0.33 M R2, less than the 0.4 M R2 of a uniform sphere. If its density became uniform, I would increase and, angular momentum being conserved, the Earth would spin more slowly and the day would grow longer.

lessons.title: Torque, Rotational Kinetic Energy and Angular Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
Torque is the turning effect of a force, τ = r x F. For rotation it plays the part that force plays for linear motion:

τ = I α

Rotational KE = (1/2) I ω2

L = I ω

  • τ — torque, α — angular acceleration
  • L — angular momentum, the rotational analogue of linear momentum p = m v; in vector form L = r x p

Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum

If no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant. Applications:

  • An ice skater spins faster when she pulls her arms in: I decreases, so ω increases to keep I ω constant. A diver tucks for the same reason.
  • Flywheels store rotational energy and smooth out the motion of machines.
  • Gyroscopes keep their axis steady and are used in navigation systems.

Worked Example: A Rotating Pulley

A 3 kg pulley of radius 30 cm rotates at 400 rev/min. Treating it as a rim (I = M R2), find its moment of inertia and its rotational kinetic energy.

Step 1: I = M R2 = 3 x (0.30)2 = 3 x 0.09 = 0.27 kg m2.

Step 2: ω = 400 rev/min = 400 x 2π / 60 = 41.9 rad s-1.

Step 3: KE = (1/2) I ω2 = (1/2) x 0.27 x (41.9)2 = 237 J.

Answer: I = 0.27 kg m2, KE = 237 J. (Note: the book prints 548 kJ, which cannot be obtained from the printed data; the step-by-step value is 237 J.)

options: tau = m a in all cases
mcqs.why: For rotation, tau = I alpha plays the part that F = m a plays for linear motion: torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

options: (1/2) m v^2 in rotational symbols only
mcqs.why: Rotational KE = (1/2) I omega^2, the analogue of (1/2) m v^2 with I replacing m and omega replacing v.

mcqs.why: Pulling her arms in decreases I; with L = I omega conserved, omega must increase, so she spins faster. A diver tucks for the same reason.

lessons.title: Weightlessness and Artificial Gravity
lessons.notes_html:
Weightlessness in a Satellite

An astronaut in orbit feels weightless, although gravity still acts on him. The satellite and the astronaut are in continuous free fall around the Earth: both fall towards the Earth with the same centripetal acceleration, so no normal reaction acts between them.

  • Weight is the normal reaction N from a supporting surface. The condition of weightlessness is N = 0.
  • Weightlessness needs: free fall (only gravity acting), N = 0, and the body and its support sharing the same acceleration — as in an orbiting satellite or a freely falling lift.

Artificial Gravity

A rotating spacecraft can produce artificial gravity: the wall of the rotating rim pushes the astronaut towards the centre, supplying the centripetal force, and the astronaut feels this push as weight. For artificial gravity equal to g:

v = √(g R)

f = (1 / 2π) √(g / R)

  • R — radius of the spacecraft, f — frequency of rotation

Worked Example: A Rotating Spacecraft

At what speed must the outer rim of a spacecraft of radius 60 m rotate to produce artificial gravity of 9.8 m s-2? Also find its time period of rotation.

Step 1: v = √(g R) = √(9.8 x 60) = √588 = 24.2 m s-1.

Step 2: T = 2π R / v = (2π x 60) / 24.2 = 15.6 s.

Answer: rim speed 24.2 m s-1, period 15.6 s. (Note: the book prints 42.2 m s-1, which would give a period of 8.9 s, not 15.6 s; the pair above is consistent.)

Key Points

  • Angles are measured in degrees, radians or revolutions; the radian is the SI unit and S = r θ.
  • Linear and angular variables: v = r ω, at = r α, ac = v2 / r = r ω2.
  • Centripetal force Fc = m v2 / r acts towards the centre, does no work, and is supplied by a real force such as gravity or tension.
  • Moment of inertia I = Σ m r2 grows with mass and with the square of the distance from the axis.
  • τ = I α, rotational KE = (1/2) I ω2, angular momentum L = I ω.
  • With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved — the spinning skater speeds up as I falls.
  • Weightlessness means the normal reaction is zero, as in a freely falling satellite.
  • Artificial gravity from rotation: v = √(g R) and f = (1 / 2π) √(g / R).

lessons.title: Classification of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
A solid has a definite shape and volume: its atoms are closely packed with strong forces between them. Solids fall into three classes, according to how their atoms, molecules or ions are arranged.

Crystalline Solids

  • The particles are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern in three dimensions, which can be studied by X-ray diffraction.
  • Examples: copper, iron, diamond, common salt (the NaCl crystal has a regular cubic structure).
  • They have sharp melting points and definite cleavage planes. Copper is a crystalline solid.
  • On heating, the distance between the molecules of a crystal increases as the crystal expands.

Amorphous Solids

  • The particles are arranged randomly, with no long-range order — like a liquid frozen in place.
  • Examples: glass, plastics, rubber. They are also called glassy solids, after glass.
  • They have no sharp melting point: they soften gradually over a range of temperature, flow extremely slowly, and break with an irregular fracture.

Polymeric Solids

  • They are built of long chains of repeated molecular units — neither perfectly regular nor fully random.
  • Examples: polythene, nylon, PVC. They are flexible, light and can be moulded.

lessons.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
The mechanical properties of a solid describe how it responds to applied forces:

  • Elasticity — regaining the original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
  • Plasticity — keeping a permanent deformation after the force is removed.
  • Strength — the maximum stress the material can bear before it breaks.
  • Stiffness — resistance to deformation, measured by the elastic modulus.
  • Hardness — resistance to scratching or indentation.
  • Ductility — the ability to be drawn into wires, as copper is.
  • Brittleness — breaking without appreciable deformation, as glass does. A body that breaks just after crossing the elastic limit is brittle.
  • Toughness — the energy absorbed before fracture.

Steel is strong, stiff and ductile, while glass is hard but brittle.

Elasticity versus Plasticity

A spring shows elasticity: remove the force and it returns completely to its original shape, provided the elastic limit was not crossed. A bent copper wire shows plasticity: the bend remains even when the force is gone.

Surprisingly, iron is more elastic than rubber. Elasticity is measured by the elastic modulus (stress / strain), not by how far a material stretches: iron needs a huge stress for a tiny strain (Young's modulus about 2 x 1011 Pa), while rubber stretches easily under a small stress (modulus about 107 Pa). Rubber is more stretchable, but iron is more elastic in the scientific sense.

lessons.title: Stress and Its Kinds
lessons.notes_html:
When a force deforms a solid, an internal restoring force is developed inside it. Stress is this restoring force per unit area:

Stress = F / A

  • F — applied force, A — cross-sectional area
  • The unit of stress is the pascal (Pa): 1 Pa = 1 N m-2.

Kinds of Stress

  • Tensile stress — the forces pull outwards, increasing the length.
  • Compressive stress — the forces push inwards, decreasing the length.

lessons.notes_html:
Strain is the fractional deformation produced by a stress:

lessons.title: Hooke's Law and the Elastic Moduli
lessons.notes_html:
Hooke's Law

Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain. The constant ratio is the elastic modulus (coefficient of elasticity):

Modulus = stress / strain

  • The modulus measures stiffness: the larger the modulus, the larger the stress needed for a given strain.

The Three Elastic Moduli

ModulusDefinitionDeformation
Young's modulus Ylongitudinal stress / longitudinal strainchange of length
Bulk modulus Kvolumetric stress / volumetric strainchange of volume
Shear modulus Gtangential stress / shear strainchange of shape

Worked Example: Stress, Strain and Young's Modulus

An iron rod 4 m long and 0.5 cm2 in cross-section stretches by 0.5 mm when a mass of 115 kg is hung from its lower end. Compute the stress, the strain and Young's modulus.

Step 1: Force F = m g = 115 x 9.8 = 1127 N. Area A = 0.5 cm2 = 0.5 x 10-4 m2. Stress = F / A = 1127 / (0.5 x 10-4) = 2.254 x 107 Pa.

Step 2: Strain = ΔL / L = 0.5 x 10-3 / 4 = 1.25 x 10-4.

Step 3: Y = stress / strain = 2.254 x 107 / 1.25 x 10-4 = 1.8 x 1011 Pa.

Answer: stress 2.254 x 107 Pa, strain 1.25 x 10-4, Y = 1.8 x 1011 Pa. (Note: the book prints the stress as 2.254 x 1011 Pa, which is 10,000 times too large; the value above gives exactly the book's Young's modulus.)

Worked Example: Angle of Shear

Two parallel and opposite forces, each 4000 N, are applied tangentially to the upper and lower faces of a cubical metal block 25 cm on a side. Find the angle of shear. (Shear modulus = 80 GPa.)

Step 1: Face area A = 0.25 x 0.25 = 0.0625 m2. Shear stress = F / A = 4000 / 0.0625 = 6.4 x 104 Pa.

Step 2: Shear strain = stress / G = 6.4 x 104 / (80 x 109) = 8 x 10-7 rad.

Answer: angle of shear = 8 x 10-7 rad. (Note: the book prints 8 x 10-5 rad, which is 100 times too large.)

Worked Example: Change in Volume

Calculate the change in volume of a solid cube 50 mm on each edge when it is subjected to a stress of 25 MPa. (Bulk modulus of copper = 125 GPa.)

Step 1: Volume V = 503 = 125,000 mm3. Volumetric strain = stress / K = 25 x 106 / (125 x 109) = 2 x 10-4.

Step 2: ΔV = strain x V = 2 x 10-4 x 125,000 = 25 mm3.

Answer: the volume decreases by 25 mm3.

lessons.title: The Stress-Strain Graph
lessons.notes_html:
The stress-strain graph summarises the whole behaviour of a material under increasing load:

  • At first the graph is a straight line: stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law region).
  • The elastic limit is the maximum stress from which the body still recovers completely.
  • Beyond it lies the plastic region, where deformation becomes permanent.
  • The yield strength (yield point) is the stress at which plastic deformation clearly begins; beyond it, removing the load leaves a permanent strain.
  • The ultimate strength is the highest point of the curve — the maximum stress the material can bear. Beyond it the material necks down and reaches the fracture point, where it breaks.
  • The yield strength is always less than the ultimate strength. The area under the whole curve measures the toughness of the material.

Key Points

  • Solids are crystalline (regular pattern, sharp melting point), amorphous (random, glassy) or polymeric (long chains).
  • Elasticity is regaining shape; plasticity is keeping a permanent deformation.
  • Stress = F / A, in pascals; it may be tensile, compressive or shearing.
  • Strain is a pure ratio with no unit and no dimensions.
  • Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain; their ratio is the elastic modulus.
  • Young's modulus is for length, bulk modulus for volume, shear modulus for shape.
  • On the stress-strain graph: straight Hooke region, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate strength, fracture.
  • Iron is scientifically more elastic than rubber because its modulus is far larger.

lessons.title: Archimedes' Principle and Floatation
lessons.notes_html:
A fluid is a substance that flows and takes the shape of its container; liquids and gases are fluids.

Archimedes' Principle

When a body is wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force (upthrust) equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it:

Fu = V ρ g

  • V — volume of fluid displaced (the immersed volume of the body)
  • ρ — density of the fluid

Law of Floatation

A body floats when the upthrust equals its weight — that is, when the weight of the displaced fluid equals the weight of the body:

  • Average density of the body less than the fluid: the body floats, partly immersed (Fu = W at equilibrium; while rising, Fu is greater than W).
  • Average density equal to the fluid: the body stays suspended anywhere in the fluid.
  • Average density greater than the fluid: the body sinks, because even the maximum upthrust (fully immersed) is less than its weight.

A heavy steel ship floats because its hollow hull encloses a large volume of air, making its average density less than that of water; the upthrust on the large displaced volume then equals the ship's weight. A hydrometer floats higher in a denser liquid, because a smaller displaced volume already balances its weight.

Liquids are practically incompressible — their molecules are already close together, so their density stays constant under pressure — while gases are compressible, because their molecules are far apart.

lessons.title: Viscosity and Drag
lessons.notes_html:
Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: the resistance between its layers to relative motion. It arises from intermolecular forces and from momentum transfer between layers moving at different speeds.

η = F / (A x velocity gradient)

  • η — coefficient of viscosity, from Newton's law of viscosity F = η A (dv / dy)
  • SI unit of η: N s m-2 (pascal-second)
  • Honey has high viscosity; water has low viscosity. The viscosity of a liquid decreases as its temperature rises.
  • No perfectly non-viscous fluid exists in nature. Liquid helium below 2.17 K becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity: it flows through the narrowest tubes without friction and creeps up and over the walls of its container.

Drag Force

A body moving through a fluid experiences a drag force opposing its motion. Drag depends on the viscosity of the fluid, the speed of the body and the shape of the body — but not on the total volume of fluid present.

Steady and Turbulent Flow

  • In steady (streamline) flow, every particle passing a given point follows the same path with the same velocity, and the pattern does not change with time. It occurs at low speeds.
  • In turbulent flow the velocity at a point keeps changing, eddies and whirls form, and the motion is disorderly. It sets in above a critical speed.

lessons.title: Terminal Velocity and Stokes' Law
lessons.notes_html:
A body falling through a fluid is pulled down by its weight and opposed by upthrust and by the viscous drag, which grows with speed. When the two upward forces together balance the weight, the net force becomes zero and the body falls at a constant terminal velocity.

Stokes' Law

For a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid, the drag is:

F = 6π η r v

  • η — coefficient of viscosity, r — radius of the sphere, v — its speed

Balancing weight = upthrust + drag at the terminal velocity gives:

vt = 2 r2 g (ρ - ρf) / (9 η)

  • Terminal velocity grows with the square of the radius and with the density difference, and falls as viscosity rises.
  • Raindrops do not hurt us because they quickly reach a small terminal velocity (about 9 m s-1 for a large drop) instead of accelerating all the way down, and their mass is tiny.
  • A parachutist likewise falls at a safe constant speed once the drag balances his weight.

lessons.title: Equation of Continuity
lessons.notes_html:
For steady flow of an incompressible fluid through a pipe, the volume passing each section per second is the same everywhere:

A1 v1 = A2 v2 = constant

  • A — cross-sectional area of the pipe, v — speed of the fluid there
  • The constant A v is the flow rate (volume per second).

The equation is derived from the law of conservation of mass: the mass entering a section per second, ρ A1 v1, must equal the mass leaving per second, ρ A2 v2, because mass is neither created nor destroyed. For an incompressible fluid the density ρ cancels.

So the fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows and slows down where it widens — as when you squeeze the end of a garden hose.

Worked Example: Speed in a Narrower Pipe

Water flows at 0.5 m s-1 in a pipe of diameter 5 cm. What is its speed in a connected pipe of diameter 2.5 cm?

Step 1: A1 v1 = A2 v2, and area is proportional to (diameter)2. So v2 = v1 x (d1 / d2)2.

Step 2: v2 = 0.5 x (5 / 2.5)2 = 0.5 x 4 = 2 m s-1.

Answer: 2 m s-1.

Worked Example: Average Speed from the Flow Rate

A pipe of diameter 10 cm delivers 5 m3 of water per hour. Find the average speed of the water.

Step 1: Area A = π (0.05)2 = 7.85 x 10-3 m2. Flow rate = 5 / 3600 = 1.39 x 10-3 m3 s-1.

Step 2: v = flow rate / A = 1.39 x 10-3 / 7.85 x 10-3 = 0.18 m s-1.

Answer: 0.18 m s-1.

lessons.title: Bernoulli's Equation
lessons.notes_html:
For steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow, the total energy of the fluid stays constant along a streamline:

P + (1/2) ρ v2 + ρ g h = constant

  • P — pressure of the fluid
  • (1/2) ρ v2 — kinetic energy per unit volume
  • ρ g h — potential energy per unit volume at height h

Bernoulli's equation is derived from the law of conservation of energy: the work done by the pressure forces on a fluid element equals the change in its kinetic and potential energy.

  • For horizontal flow it gives the key rule: where the speed is greater, the pressure is smaller, and where the fluid slows down, the pressure rises.

Worked Example: Lift on an Aeroplane Wing

An aeroplane wing is designed so that air moves across its top at 450 m s-1 and below it at 410 m s-1. Find the pressure difference between the bottom and the top of the wing. (Density of air = 1.29 kg m-3.)

Step 1: ΔP = (1/2) ρ (vtop2 - vbottom2) = (1/2) x 1.29 x (4502 - 4102).

Step 2: 4502 - 4102 = 202,500 - 168,100 = 34,400. So ΔP = 0.645 x 34,400 = 22,188 Pa.

Answer: about 22 kPa, with the greater pressure below the wing — this difference lifts the aeroplane.
