lessons.title: Applications of Bernoulli's Principle
lessons.notes_html:
Speed of Efflux (Torricelli's Theorem)

The speed with which a liquid jets out of a hole at depth h below the surface is the speed it would gain falling freely through h:

v = √(2 g h)

Worked Example: Height above a Hole

The velocity of efflux of water through an orifice is 9.9 m s-1. How high is the water surface inside the tank above the orifice?

Step 1: h = v2 / (2 g) = 9.92 / (2 x 9.8) = 98.01 / 19.6.

Answer: h = 5 m.

Venturi Meter

A Venturi meter measures the speed (flow rate) of a fluid in a pipe. The pipe narrows at a throat; the fluid speeds up there and its pressure falls. Measuring the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat gives the speed.

Filter Pump and Atomizer

  • A filter pump forces water through a constriction; the fast water has low pressure, so air is sucked in through a side tube and carried away, leaving a partial vacuum for filtration.
  • An atomizer (spray) blows air fast across the top of a tube dipped in liquid; the pressure there falls, atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up the tube, and the air stream breaks it into a fine spray.
  • The same pressure difference gives lift to an aeroplane wing and makes a spinning cricket ball swing.

Worked Example: Pressure for a Fire Hose

What gauge pressure is needed in a large fire hose if its nozzle is to shoot water straight upward to a height of 25 m?

Step 1: The jet must leave with v = √(2 g h) = √(2 x 9.8 x 25) = √490 = 22.1 m s-1.

Step 2: By Bernoulli, the gauge pressure supplies the kinetic energy per unit volume: P = (1/2) ρ v2 = (1/2) x 1000 x 490 = 2.45 x 105 Pa.

Answer: 2.45 x 105 Pa.

Key Points

  • Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle).
  • A body floats when upthrust equals its weight; it sinks when its average density exceeds the fluid's.
  • Viscosity is internal friction between fluid layers; it falls as a liquid warms up.
  • Drag on a small sphere: F = 6π η r v (Stokes' law); terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight.
  • Continuity: A1 v1 = A2 v2, from conservation of mass; fluid speeds up in a narrow section.
  • Bernoulli: P + (1/2) ρ v2 + ρ g h = constant, from conservation of energy; faster flow means lower pressure.
  • Speed of efflux v = √(2 g h); the Venturi meter, filter pump and atomizer all work on Bernoulli's principle.
  • A superfluid, like liquid helium below 2.17 K, has zero viscosity.

lessons.title: Thermal Equilibrium and the Kinetic Theory of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Two bodies in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they have exactly the same temperature, so no net heat flows between them. (Complete thermodynamic equilibrium also needs mechanical equilibrium — equal pressures — and chemical equilibrium.)

The Earth is not in thermal equilibrium with the Sun: their temperatures are vastly different (about 5800 K and 288 K) and heat flows continuously from the Sun to the Earth, while the Earth radiates heat back to space.

Assumptions of the Kinetic Theory of Gases

  • A gas consists of a very large number of tiny identical molecules in continuous random motion.
  • The molecules are point masses whose own volume is negligible compared with the container.
  • There are no intermolecular forces except during collisions.
  • All collisions, with each other and with the walls, are perfectly elastic.
  • The molecules obey Newton's laws, and a collision lasts a negligible time compared with the time between collisions.
  • The motion has no preferred direction, so the pressure is the same in all directions.

From the kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of a gas molecule depends only on the absolute temperature:

Average KE = (3/2) k T

  • k — Boltzmann's constant, T — absolute temperature in kelvin

lessons.title: Equation of State for an Ideal Gas
lessons.notes_html:
An ideal gas is one whose molecules are point masses with no volume and no forces between them. Its state is described completely by the equation of state:

P V = n R T

  • P — pressure, V — volume, n — number of moles
  • R — universal gas constant = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1
  • T — absolute temperature in kelvin

The equation combines Boyle's law (V proportional to 1/P at constant T) and Charles's law (V proportional to T at constant P): together they give V proportional to T/P, and including the amount of gas gives PV = nRT. Knowing any three of P, V, n and T fixes the fourth.

A real gas does not obey this equation exactly: its molecules have finite size and attract each other, so at high pressure and low temperature its behaviour deviates, and the van der Waals equation (with corrections for molecular volume and attraction) must be used instead.

lessons.title: Internal Energy
lessons.notes_html:
The internal energy U of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules.

  • For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so the potential energy is zero and the internal energy is purely the total kinetic energy of the molecules: U = (3/2) nRT for a monatomic gas.
  • Therefore the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature (on T and V together in the general statement of state variables).
  • Heating a gas raises the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so its internal energy rises with temperature.

lessons.title: Work and Heat: The P-V Diagram
lessons.notes_html:
Count Rumford, while boring cannon barrels, observed that friction produced large amounts of heat with no visible source: the heat produced was proportional to the mechanical work done. This showed that heat is a form of energy and can be produced by work.

W = J H

  • J — Joule's constant (the mechanical equivalent of heat) = 4.18 J per calorie; the ratio of work done to heat energy

Work on a P-V Diagram

When a gas expands or is compressed, the work done is the area under the pressure-volume (P-V) curve between the initial and final volumes.

  • Work done by the system: the gas expands, pushes the piston out, and energy leaves the system. In this book's convention it is taken as positive.
  • Work done on the system: an external agent compresses the gas and energy enters the system; it is taken as negative.
  • For expansion at constant pressure, W = P ΔV.

Worked Example: Work Done in an Isobaric Expansion

How much work is done by an ideal gas expanding from 3 litres to 33 litres against a constant pressure of 2.5 atm? (1 atm = 1.013 x 105 Pa.)

Step 1: ΔV = 33 - 3 = 30 litres = 30 x 10-3 m3. P = 2.5 x 1.013 x 105 = 2.53 x 105 Pa.

Step 2: W = P ΔV = 2.53 x 105 x 30 x 10-3 = 7.6 x 103 J.

Answer: 7.6 kJ of work is done by the gas.

lessons.title: First Law of Thermodynamics and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
The first law of thermodynamics is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat: the heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system.

Q = ΔU + W

The Four Processes

ProcessConditionFirst Law Becomes
IsothermalΔT = 0, so ΔU = 0Q = W: all the supplied heat becomes work
AdiabaticQ = 0 (no heat exchange)W = -ΔU: work is done at the cost of internal energy
IsochoricΔV = 0, so W = 0Q = ΔU: all the heat raises internal energy
IsobaricP constantQ = ΔU + P ΔV

On a P-V diagram the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve: in an adiabatic expansion no heat flows in, so the gas cools as it expands and its pressure falls faster. The adiabatic slope is γ times the isothermal slope, where γ = Cp / Cv is greater than 1.

Worked Example: Change in Internal Energy

An ideal gas expands isobarically at 2.5 kPa, its volume increasing from 2 m3 to 5 m3. If 13 kJ of energy is transferred to the gas by heat, find the change in its internal energy.

Step 1: W = P ΔV = 2500 x (5 - 2) = 7500 J = 7.5 kJ.

Step 2: ΔU = Q - W = 13 - 7.5 = 5.5 kJ.

Answer: the internal energy increases by 5.5 kJ.

lessons.title: Heat Engines and the Carnot Engine
lessons.notes_html:
A heat engine converts heat energy into mechanical work by operating in a cycle between a hot source and a cold sink: it absorbs heat QH from the source, converts part of it into work W, and rejects the rest QL to the sink. By the first law, W = QH - QL.

Efficiency η = W / QH = 1 - QL / QH

The Carnot Engine

The Carnot engine is an ideal, reversible engine: a cylinder with a frictionless piston, a hot source, a cold sink and an insulating stand. Its cycle has four strokes:

  • Isothermal expansion at the source temperature TH, absorbing heat QH.
  • Adiabatic expansion, cooling to the sink temperature TL.
  • Isothermal compression at TL, rejecting heat QL.
  • Adiabatic compression, warming back to TH.

Carnot efficiency η = 1 - TL / TH

  • This is the maximum possible efficiency for any engine working between TH and TL; no real engine can exceed it.
  • The efficiency would be 100% only if the sink were at 0 K (absolute zero), which cannot be reached.

Worked Example: A Carnot Engine

A Carnot engine has a source at 227 °C and a sink at 127 °C. Find its efficiency, and the heat taken from the source and rejected to the sink when 10,000 J of work is done.

Step 1: TH = 227 + 273 = 500 K; TL = 127 + 273 = 400 K. η = 1 - 400 / 500 = 0.20 = 20%.

Step 2: QH = W / η = 10,000 / 0.20 = 5 x 104 J.

Step 3: QL = QH - W = 50,000 - 10,000 = 4 x 104 J.

Answer: efficiency 20%, heat input 5 x 104 J, heat rejected 4 x 104 J.

mcqs.why: By the first law applied to the cycle, the work output is the difference between heat absorbed and heat rejected: W = QH - QL.

lessons.title: Refrigerator and Coefficient of Performance
lessons.notes_html:
A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: it transfers heat from a cold body to a hot body by spending external work.

  • The refrigerant absorbs heat QL from the cold chamber.
  • The compressor does work W on it.
  • It rejects heat QH = QL + W to the surroundings — which is why the back of a refrigerator feels warm.

COP = QL / W

  • For a Carnot refrigerator, COP = TL / (TH - TL).
  • Unlike efficiency, the COP can be greater than 1: a refrigerator moves more heat than the work it consumes.

mcqs.q: A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: it
options: transfers heat from a cold body to a hot body by spending external work
destroys heat inside the cold chamber
mcqs.why: A refrigerator transfers heat from cold to hot by spending external work: the refrigerant absorbs QL from the cold chamber and rejects QH = QL + W outside.

mcqs.q: The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is
options: COP = QH / W always less than 1
mcqs.why: COP = QL / W: the heat removed from the cold chamber divided by the work spent — it measures how much cooling each joule of work buys.

mcqs.why: For a Carnot refrigerator, COP = TL / (TH - TL), using the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs.

options: can be greater than 1: a refrigerator moves more heat than the work it consumes
mcqs.why: Unlike efficiency, the COP can exceed 1 because the refrigerator moves more heat (QL) than the work (W) it consumes.

options: it rejects heat QH = QL + W to the surroundings
the motor is inefficient by design

mcqs.why: The refrigerant rejects QH = QL + W to the surroundings at the back, which is why the back of a refrigerator feels warm.

mcqs.why: The refrigerant absorbs QL from the cold chamber; the compressor does work W on it; it then rejects QH = QL + W to the surroundings.

mcqs.why: QH = QL + W = 650 + 100 = 750 J: the heat dumped outside is the heat removed plus the work input.

mcqs.q: A refrigerator cannot work with W = 0 because that would mean
options: the COP would be less than 1
heat flowing by itself from cold to hot, which the second law forbids
the first law would be broken by cooling
mcqs.why: Moving heat from a cold body to a hot body requires external work; heat never flows that way by itself (second law).

lessons.title: Second Law, Entropy and Reversible Processes
lessons.notes_html:
The second law of thermodynamics gives the proper direction of the flow of heat: heat flows by itself from a hot body to a cold body, never the reverse, and no engine can convert all its heat into work.

Entropy

Entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system, and of how much of its energy is unavailable for work. For a reversible change:

ΔS = Q / T

  • A reversible process passes through a continuous sequence of equilibrium states, infinitely slowly, and can be exactly reversed with no change in the system or the surroundings. Over a reversible cycle the total entropy change is zero: entropy is a state function.
  • An irreversible process is a real, spontaneous process — free expansion, friction, heat flow across a finite temperature difference. It cannot be reversed without leaving changes elsewhere, and it always increases the total entropy of the universe.

Worked Example: Entropy Change on Freezing

336 J of energy is needed to melt 1 g of ice at 0 °C. Find the change in entropy when 30 g of water at 0 °C is changed to ice at 0 °C by a refrigerator.

Step 1: Heat removed Q = 30 x 336 = 10,080 J, at T = 273 K.

Step 2: ΔS = -Q / T = -10,080 / 273 = -36.8 J K-1 (negative, because heat leaves the water).

Answer: the entropy of the water decreases by 36.8 J K-1; the surroundings gain more entropy than this, so the total entropy of the universe still increases.

Heat Death of the Universe

Because entropy always increases, the universe is heading towards a state of maximum entropy — the heat death — in which the temperature is uniform everywhere, no temperature differences remain to drive engines or do work, and all physical processes effectively cease.

Key Points

  • Thermal equilibrium means equal temperatures and no net heat flow.
  • Kinetic theory: molecules are point masses in random motion with elastic collisions; average KE = (3/2) k T.
  • Ideal gas: PV = nRT; real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
  • The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.
  • Work done is the area under the P-V curve; W = J H with J = 4.18 J per calorie.
  • First law: Q = ΔU + W. Isothermal: Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0. Isochoric: W = 0.
  • Heat engine efficiency η = 1 - QL / QH; Carnot efficiency 1 - TL / TH is the maximum possible.
  • A refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot using work; COP = QL / W.
  • Second law: heat flows from hot to cold; entropy of the universe always increases in real processes.

heat flows by itself from a hot body to a cold body, never the reverse, and no engine can convert all its heat into work
engines can be 100% efficient with good design
mcqs.why: The second law gives the proper direction of heat flow — hot to cold, never the reverse by itself — and forbids converting all heat into work.

increases the entropy of the universe

always increases the total entropy of the universe

mcqs.q: Over a complete reversible cycle, the total entropy change is

mcqs.q: The heat death of the universe refers to a state of

mcqs.why: Because entropy always increases, the universe heads towards maximum entropy — uniform temperature, no differences to drive engines, and all physical processes effectively cease.

mcqs.q: Melting 1 g of ice at 0 °C needs 336 J. The entropy increase of the ice on melting is
mcqs.why: delta S = Q / T = 336 / 273 = 1.23 J K-1 for 1 g melting reversibly at 273 K.

options: whether the process is reversible in practice
the initial and final states, not on the path
the work done along the way
mcqs.why: Like internal energy, entropy is fixed by the state: over any cycle returning to the start state, the total entropy change is zero.

lessons.title: Wave Basics and the Principle of Superposition
lessons.notes_html:
A wave carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter. For a periodic wave:

v = f λ

T f = 1

  • v — wave speed, f — frequency, λ — wavelength, T — time period

Principle of Superposition

When two or more waves pass through the same region at the same time, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the individual displacements of the waves at that point. After overlapping, the waves pass through each other unchanged. This one principle explains interference, beats and standing waves.

Worked Example: Speed and Frequency of a Wave

A pulse of a transverse wave on a string moves 15 m in 0.075 s. If the wavelength is 0.8 m, find (a) the velocity of the pulse and (b) the frequency of the wave.

Step 1: v = distance / time = 15 / 0.075 = 200 m s-1.

Step 2: f = v / λ = 200 / 0.8 = 250 Hz.

Answer: (a) 200 m s-1 (b) 250 Hz.

Worked Example: Wavelength of a Radio Wave

Find the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave of frequency 600 kHz travelling at 3 x 108 m s-1.

Step 1: λ = v / f = 3 x 108 / (600 x 103) = 3 x 108 / 6 x 105.

Answer: λ = 500 m.

lessons.title: Interference of Waves
lessons.notes_html:
Interference is the superposition of two waves of the same frequency travelling in the same region, producing a steady pattern of strong and weak regions. Only the amplitude (and so the loudness or brightness) changes from place to place; the frequency, wavelength and time period of the resultant pattern stay the same.

  • Constructive interference: the waves arrive in phase (path difference = n λ, where n = 0, 1, 2, ...). Their displacements add, giving maximum amplitude and maximum loudness.
  • Destructive interference: the waves arrive in opposite phase (path difference = (n + 1/2) λ). Their displacements cancel, giving minimum amplitude and quiet regions.
  • Interference needs coherent sources: sources with a constant phase relationship.

Interference does not destroy energy. Energy is only redistributed: the bright regions gain more than the average, the dark regions less, and the total energy over the whole region is unchanged.

options: a pattern whose frequency varies from place to place
a steady pattern of strong and weak regions, with only the amplitude varying from place to place
mcqs.why: Only the amplitude (loudness or brightness) changes from place to place; the frequency, wavelength and period of the resultant pattern stay the same.

mcqs.q: Destructive interference occurs when the waves arrive in opposite phase, with path difference
mcqs.why: In opposite phase (path difference = (n + 1/2) lambda) the displacements cancel, giving minimum amplitude and quiet regions.

mcqs.why: Interference needs coherent sources: sources with a constant phase relationship, so the pattern stays steady.

mcqs.why: Energy is only redistributed by interference; the total energy over the whole region is unchanged.

lessons.title: Beats
lessons.notes_html:
Beats are the periodic rising and falling of loudness heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies are sounded together. As the waves drift in and out of phase, the resultant amplitude rises and falls.

Beat frequency = | f1 - f2 |

  • If the two frequencies differ by 2 Hz, two beats are heard every second.
  • Beats cannot be detected if the frequency difference is more than about 10 Hz: the ear's persistence of hearing is about 0.1 s, so faster beats merge into a single rough tone.

Uses of Beats

  • Tuning musical instruments: the instrument is adjusted until the beats against a standard fork disappear.
  • Finding an unknown frequency from a known one.
  • Detecting the speed of moving objects (Doppler beats in radar and sonar).

Worked Example: Frequency from Beats

Two tuning forks A and B produce 14 beats in 2 seconds. The frequency of A is 512 Hz. When a little wax is attached to the prongs of B, the beats disappear. Find the frequency of B.

Step 1: Beat frequency = 14 / 2 = 7 Hz, so B is either 512 + 7 = 519 Hz or 512 - 7 = 505 Hz.

Step 2: Wax lowers the frequency of B. The beats disappear, so B's frequency fell towards 512 Hz — B must have started above 512 Hz.

Answer: B = 519 Hz.

options: two waves of exactly the same frequency meet
a single wave reflects from a wall
two waves have very different frequencies
two sound waves of slightly different frequencies are sounded together
mcqs.why: As the waves drift in and out of phase, the resultant amplitude rises and falls — the phenomenon of beats.

mcqs.why: Beat frequency = | f1 - f2 |: if the frequencies differ by 2 Hz, two beats are heard every second.

mcqs.why: The ear's persistence of hearing is about 0.1 s, so beats faster than about 10 per second merge into a single rough tone.

mcqs.why: Wax adds mass to the prongs and lowers the fork's frequency — the key step in deciding whether B was 519 or 505 Hz.

mcqs.why: The listed uses of beats: tuning instruments, finding an unknown frequency from a known one, and detecting speeds via Doppler beats in radar and sonar.

mcqs.why: Beat frequency = | f1 - f2 | = 2 Hz means two beats are heard every second, as the notes state directly.

options: rises and falls periodically, producing the beats
mcqs.why: The waves drift in and out of phase, so the resultant amplitude rises and falls — heard as periodic rising and falling of loudness.

lessons.title: Stationary Waves in a Stretched String
lessons.notes_html:
A stationary (standing) wave is formed when two identical waves travel in opposite directions along the same string and superpose. Points called nodes stay permanently at rest; points called antinodes vibrate with maximum amplitude. The distance between a node and the next antinode is λ/4.

  • A standing wave does not transfer energy: the pattern does not move along the string, and energy merely oscillates between kinetic and potential forms within each segment between nodes.

Waves on a Stretched String

v = √(T / μ)

  • T — tension in the string, μ — mass per unit length

For a string of length L fixed at both ends, stationary waves form only at certain frequencies, with nodes at the fixed ends:

fn = n v / (2 L)

  • The fundamental (first harmonic) has one loop: λ = 2L and f1 = v / (2L).
  • The second harmonic has two loops (f2 = 2 f1), the third has three loops, and so on.
  • Plucking or bowing excites a mixture of harmonics, which gives the string its tone quality.

Worked Example: Harmonics of a Long String

An 80 m long stretched string has mass per unit length 9 x 10-3 kg m-1 and tension 20 N. Find its fundamental frequency and the next three frequencies.

Step 1: v = √(T / μ) = √(20 / (9 x 10-3)) = √2222 = 47.1 m s-1.

Step 2: f1 = v / (2L) = 47.1 / 160 = 0.295 Hz.

Step 3: The harmonics are multiples: f2 = 0.59 Hz, f3 = 0.885 Hz, f4 = 1.18 Hz.

Answer: 0.295 Hz, 0.59 Hz, 0.885 Hz and 1.18 Hz.

lessons.title: Stationary Waves in Air Columns
lessons.notes_html:
Stationary waves also form in the air inside pipes, with the ends of the pipe fixing the boundary conditions.

Pipe Open at Both Ends

  • There is an antinode at each open end.
  • All harmonics are present: fn = n v / (2L), for n = 1, 2, 3, ...

Pipe Closed at One End

  • There is a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
  • Only odd harmonics occur: fn = (2n - 1) v / (4L), for n = 1, 2, 3, ...
  • The fundamental of a closed pipe is half that of an open pipe of the same length, so the ratio of the fundamental of an open pipe to that of a closed pipe is 2 : 1.

Worked Example: An Open Organ Pipe

The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe 100 cm long is 180 Hz. Find the speed of sound in the pipe and the frequency of the second harmonic.

Step 1: For an open pipe, f1 = v / (2L), so v = 2 L f1 = 2 x 1.0 x 180 = 360 m s-1.

Step 2: Second harmonic f2 = 2 f1 = 360 Hz. (This is the first overtone; the second overtone is the third harmonic, 540 Hz.)

Answer: v = 360 m s-1, second harmonic 360 Hz.

options: a node at each open end
an antinode at each open end, and all harmonics are present: fn = n v / (2 L)
a node at one end and antinode at the other
mcqs.why: Open pipe: antinode at each open end, all harmonics present, fn = n v / (2L) for n = 1, 2, 3, ...

options: a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, and only odd harmonics occur
mcqs.why: Closed pipe: node at the closed end, antinode at the open end; only odd harmonics occur: fn = (2n - 1) v / (4L).

mcqs.why: Only odd harmonics occur in a closed pipe, so fn = (2n - 1) v / (4L): f1 = v / 4L, then 3 v / 4L, 5 v / 4L, ...

mcqs.why: Air at an open end is free to move (antinode); air at a closed end cannot move (node). These boundary conditions select the allowed harmonics.

lessons.title: Diffraction of Waves
lessons.notes_html:
Diffraction is the bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle or through a slit, so that the wave spreads into the shadow region.

Conditions for Noticeable Diffraction

  • The size of the obstacle or aperture must be comparable to the wavelength: if it is much larger than λ, the wave passes almost straight on with a sharp shadow.
  • The waves must be coherent, keeping a constant phase relationship, so the diffracted waves interfere steadily.
  • The wave must meet a sharp edge, slit or obstacle that bends part of the wavefront.

This is why we can hear sound around corners (the wavelength of sound is comparable to doors and walls) but cannot see around them (the wavelength of light is far too small).

mcqs.q: Diffraction is
options: the reflection of waves from a surface
the bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle or through a slit, spreading into the shadow region
the change of frequency from a moving source
mcqs.why: Diffraction bends waves around edges or through slits so the wave spreads into the shadow region.

mcqs.q: Diffraction is most noticeable when the size of the obstacle or aperture is
options: much smaller than the wavelength in all cases
mcqs.why: If the obstacle is much larger than lambda, the wave passes almost straight on with a sharp shadow; comparable sizes give noticeable diffraction.

mcqs.q: If an obstacle is much larger than the wavelength, the wave
options: passes almost straight on with a sharp shadow

lessons.title: Doppler Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source moves relative to the observer.

Approaching: f' = f v / (v - vs)

Receding: f' = f v / (v + vs)

  • f' — observed frequency, f — true frequency, v — wave speed, vs — speed of the source
  • For an approaching source the observed wavelength shortens: λ' = λ (1 - vs / v), and the frequency rises. For a receding source the wavelength lengthens and the frequency falls.
  • When the observer moves instead, f' = f (v ± vo) / v: plus when moving towards the source, minus when moving away.

Worked Example: A Passing Car Horn

A car travelling at 90 km h-1 sounds its horn of frequency 800 Hz. What frequency does a stationary listener hear (a) as the car approaches and (b) after it has passed? (Speed of sound = 340 m s-1.)

Step 1: vs = 90 km h-1 = 25 m s-1.

Step 2: Approaching: f' = 800 x 340 / (340 - 25) = 272,000 / 315 = 863.5 Hz.

Step 3: Receding: f' = 800 x 340 / (340 + 25) = 272,000 / 365 = 745 Hz.

Answer: (a) 863.5 Hz (b) 745 Hz. Applications of the Doppler effect include radar speed traps, sonar, medical ultrasound and the red shift of distant galaxies.

options: the bending of waves around an obstacle
the restriction of vibrations to one plane
the superposition of two waves of slightly different frequency
the apparent change in the frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source moves relative to the observer
mcqs.why: Relative motion between source and observer changes the observed frequency and wavelength: approaching raises f, receding lowers it.

lessons.title: Polarization of Light
lessons.notes_html:
Polarization is the restriction of the vibrations of a transverse wave to a single plane. Only transverse waves can be polarized — this is the phenomenon that proves light is a transverse wave. Sound waves, being longitudinal, cannot be polarized.

Producing Polarized Light

  • Polaroid sheet: it absorbs the vibrations in all planes except one. Unpolarized light of intensity I emerges plane-polarized with intensity I/2.
  • Reflection at Brewster's angle: the reflected light is fully polarized.
  • Double refraction in calcite, which splits light into ordinary and extraordinary rays.
  • Scattering by small particles.

Detecting Polarized Light

A second Polaroid (the analyser) detects polarization: rotating it makes the transmitted intensity of plane-polarized light vary from maximum down to zero (extinction), while unpolarized light only dims to half intensity however the analyser is turned.

Stressed Materials and Photoelasticity

A transparent material under mechanical stress becomes doubly refracting (the photoelastic effect): it splits light into two rays travelling at different speeds, producing coloured fringe patterns between crossed polarizers. The pattern shows where the stress is greatest, so stressed models are used in engineering to study stresses in structures.

Two More Wave Facts

  • Reflection at a boundary: a wave reflected from a denser medium changes phase by π; reflected back into the rarer medium there is effectively no change (2π).
  • An accelerated mass produces gravitational waves. Light escaping from a strong gravitational field loses energy and its wavelength grows — the gravitational red shift, a prediction of general relativity.

Key Points

  • v = f λ and T f = 1 for every periodic wave.
  • Superposition: the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.
  • Interference: constructive at path difference n λ, destructive at (n + 1/2) λ; energy is redistributed, never lost.
  • Beats: beat frequency = | f1 - f2 |; used for tuning instruments and finding unknown frequencies.
  • Standing waves have fixed nodes and antinodes (λ/4 apart) and transfer no energy.
  • String: fn = n v / (2L) with v = √(T / μ). Open pipe: all harmonics; closed pipe: odd harmonics only.
  • Doppler effect: approaching source raises the observed frequency, receding source lowers it.
  • Diffraction is strong when the obstacle or slit is comparable in size to the wavelength.
  • Only transverse waves can be polarized; polarization proves light is transverse. A Polaroid halves unpolarized light.

lessons.title: Coulomb's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them:

F = k Q1 Q2 / r2

  • k = 1 / (4π ε0) = 9 x 109 N m2 C-2 in free space
  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
  • The force on each charge is equal and opposite (Newton's third law), and forces from many charges add by superposition.
  • The charge on an electron or a proton is 1.6 x 10-19 C.
  • In a material medium the force is reduced by the relative permittivity εr, which for static fields is always greater than one (it equals one only for vacuum).

Worked Example: Force Between Two Charged Coins

Two coins lie 2 m apart on a table and carry equal charges. Each experiences a force of 3 N. Find the charge on each coin.

Step 1: F = k Q2 / r2, so Q = r √(F / k).

Step 2: Q = 2 x √(3 / (9 x 109)) = 2 x √(3.33 x 10-10) = 2 x 1.83 x 10-5.

Answer: Q = 3.65 x 10-5 C on each coin.

mcqs.why: Coulomb's law: F = k Q1 Q2 / r^2, acting along the line joining the charges; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

mcqs.why: F is directly proportional to the product of the charges, so doubling one charge doubles the force.

mcqs.why: The total force is the vector sum of the forces from each charge separately — the principle of superposition.

lessons.title: Electric Field and Electric Field Intensity
lessons.notes_html:
An electric field is the region around a charge in which another charge experiences a force. The electric field intensity at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there:

E = F / q

E = k Q / r2

  • E — field intensity, unit N C-1 (the same as V m-1)
  • The direction of E is the direction of the force on a small positive test charge: away from a positive charge, towards a negative charge.
  • The total field of many charges is the vector sum of their separate fields.
  • A charged conducting sphere acts, at every point outside it, exactly like a point charge of the same total charge placed at its centre, because all its charge sits on the outer surface.

Electric Lines of Force

  • They start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity).
  • They never intersect: at a crossing point the field would need two directions at once, which is impossible — the tangent to a line gives the one direction of the field.
  • They are close together where the field is strong and far apart where it is weak.
  • They meet a charged surface at right angles, and they do not pass through a conductor.

Worked Example: Field of a Charged Sphere

A hollow metallic sphere of diameter 10 cm carries a charge of 80 μC. Find the electric intensity (a) 60 cm from its centre and (b) at its surface.

Step 1: Outside the sphere it acts as a point charge at the centre. E = k Q / r2 = 9 x 109 x 80 x 10-6 / r2 = 7.2 x 105 / r2.

Step 2: (a) At r = 0.60 m: E = 7.2 x 105 / 0.36 = 2 x 106 N C-1.

Step 3: (b) At the surface, r = 0.05 m: E = 7.2 x 105 / 0.0025 = 2.88 x 108 N C-1.

Answer: (a) 2 x 106 N C-1 (b) 2.88 x 108 N C-1.

lessons.title: The Faraday Cage: Zero Field Inside a Conductor
lessons.notes_html:
In electrostatic equilibrium the electric field inside a conductor is zero: if it were not, the free charges in the conductor would keep moving until it became zero.

How the Cage Works

  • A Faraday cage is a hollow conductor that shields its interior from external electric fields.
  • When an external field is applied, the free charges redistribute on the outer surface of the cage until their own field exactly cancels the applied field everywhere inside.
  • The resultant field inside the hollow cage is therefore E = 0, and anyone or anything inside is protected from the external field — which is why a car is a safe place in a thunderstorm.
  • Inside a hollow charged sphere the field is likewise zero; all the charge resides on the outer surface.

the same as at the surface

lessons.title: Electric Potential and Potential Gradient
lessons.notes_html:
The electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in bringing a small positive test charge from infinity to that point:

V = W / q

  • Potential is a scalar; its unit is the volt (1 V = 1 J C-1).

The potential gradient is the rate of change of potential with distance. The field is its negative:

E = - ΔV / Δd

  • The field points in the direction of decreasing potential.
  • Between parallel plates the field is uniform: E = ΔV / Δd.

The Electron Volt

One electron volt (1 eV) is the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt. It is a unit of energy: 1 eV = 1.6 x 10-19 C x 1 V = 1.6 x 10-19 J.

Worked Example: Field Between Two Plates

The potential difference between two metal plates is 120 V and their separation is 3 mm. Find the electric field between the plates.

Step 1: E = ΔV / Δd = 120 / (3 x 10-3) = 120 / 0.003.

Answer: E = 40,000 V m-1 = 40 kV m-1.

lessons.title: Motion of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Electric Field
lessons.notes_html:
A charged particle in a uniform electric field feels a constant force and therefore has a constant acceleration:

F = q E

a = q E / m

  • If the particle enters along the field, it speeds up or slows down in a straight line.
  • If it enters perpendicular to the field, it follows a parabolic path, exactly like a projectile under gravity: uniform motion along its original direction combined with uniformly accelerated motion along the field.
  • The deflection after travelling a length L at speed v is:

y = (1/2) (q E / m) (L / v)2

  • A positive charge is deflected towards the negative plate; a negative charge (such as an electron) towards the positive plate.
  • This principle is used in cathode-ray tubes and inkjet printers.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
A steady current is a current whose magnitude and direction do not change with time. Current is the rate of flow of charge:

I = Q / t

  • The conventional direction of current is the direction of flow of positive charge — from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the source — opposite to the actual flow of electrons.
  • Sources of current maintain a potential difference: cells and batteries (chemical energy), generators (mechanical energy), solar cells (light energy) and thermocouples (heat energy).

Drift of Free Electrons

In a metal, free electrons move randomly at high speed with no net flow. When a potential difference is applied, a small drift velocity is added to this random motion, opposite to the field direction (electrons are negative). This slow, steady drift of the whole electron gas — typically only millimetres per second — is the electric current.

Current in Electrolytes and Plasmas

In an electrolyte or a plasma, current is carried by ions, not electrons alone: positive ions (cations) drift towards the cathode and negative ions (anions) towards the anode, and both streams contribute to the current. In a plasma, free electrons and positive ions both carry the current.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
lessons.notes_html:
Ohm's Law

At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it:

V = I R

  • R — resistance of the conductor, in ohms (Ω)
  • Ohmic materials obey the law: their V-I graph is a straight line through the origin (metals at constant temperature).
  • Non-ohmic materials do not: filament lamps (resistance rises as the filament heats), diodes (current flows mainly one way) and thermistors.

Resistivity and Conductivity

R = ρ L / A

  • ρ — resistivity: the resistance of a 1 m cube of the material, unit Ω m. It depends on the material and its temperature, not on the shape of the sample.
  • Doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance; doubling the area halves it.
  • Conductivity σ = 1 / ρ, unit Ω-1 m-1: it measures how easily a material conducts. Metals have low resistivity; insulators very high.

Worked Example: Potential Difference from Charge Flow

Calculate the potential difference across a wire of resistance 5 Ω if a charge of 720 C passes through it per minute.

Step 1: I = Q / t = 720 / 60 = 12 A.

Step 2: V = I R = 12 x 5 = 60 V.

Answer: 60 V.

Worked Example: Resistivity of a Wire

A 10 m long wire of diameter 0.2 cm has a resistance of 3 Ω. Find the resistivity of its material and its conductivity.

Step 1: Radius r = 0.1 cm = 10-3 m. Area A = π r2 = 3.14 x 10-6 m2.

Step 2: ρ = R A / L = 3 x 3.14 x 10-6 / 10 = 9.4 x 10-7 Ω m.

Step 3: σ = 1 / ρ = 1 / (9.4 x 10-7) = 1.06 x 106 Ω-1 m-1.

Answer: ρ = 9.4 x 10-7 Ω m, σ = 1.06 x 106 Ω-1 m-1.

lessons.title: Effect of Temperature: Thermistor and LDR
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature Coefficient of Resistance

  • Positive coefficient (metals): resistance increases as temperature rises, because the hotter atoms vibrate more and scatter the drifting electrons more often.
  • Negative coefficient (semiconductors, insulators, thermistors): resistance decreases as temperature rises, because heating frees many more charge carriers, and this outweighs the extra scattering.

The Thermistor

A thermistor is a semiconductor device whose resistance changes sharply with temperature; the common type has a negative coefficient, so its resistance falls rapidly as it warms. Uses in daily life:

  • Temperature measurement and control: thermostats and digital thermometers.
  • Fire alarms: a sudden rise in temperature changes the resistance and triggers the alarm.
  • Automatic temperature compensation in circuits, and liquid-level indicators.

The Light Dependent Resistor (LDR)

An LDR is a semiconductor whose resistance decreases when the intensity of light falling on it increases, because the light frees more charge carriers. LDRs are used in automatic street lights, light meters and burglar alarms.

options: decreases, because heating frees many more charge carriers, outweighing the extra scattering
mcqs.why: Heating frees many more charge carriers in semiconductors, insulators and thermistors, and this outweighs the extra scattering, so resistance decreases.

lessons.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel
lessons.notes_html:
Series Connection

The same current flows through every resistor, and the total potential difference is the sum of the separate drops, so the equivalent resistance is the sum:

R = R1 + R2 + R3

  • The series equivalent is always larger than any single resistor in the chain.

Parallel Connection

The same potential difference is across every resistor, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents:

1 / R = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + 1 / R3

  • The parallel equivalent is always smaller than the smallest resistor in the group.
  • Household appliances are wired in parallel so that each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently.

mcqs.q: For resistors in series, the equivalent resistance is
options: R = R1 + R2 + R3, the sum of the separate resistances
mcqs.why: In series the same current flows through every resistor and the total p.d. is the sum of the drops, so the equivalent resistance is the sum.

mcqs.q: For resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance is given by
options: R = (R1 R2 R3) / (R1 + R2 + R3) in all cases
mcqs.why: In parallel the same p.d. is across every resistor and the total current is the sum of the branch currents, giving 1 / R = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + 1 / R3.

mcqs.why: Series resistances add, so the equivalent is always larger than any single resistor in the chain.

mcqs.q: The parallel equivalent resistance is always
options: smaller than the smallest resistor in the group
mcqs.why: Adding parallel paths always lowers the total resistance below that of the smallest single resistor in the group.

mcqs.why: The same potential difference is across every parallel resistor, while the total current is the sum of the branch currents.

mcqs.why: Parallel wiring gives each appliance the full supply voltage and lets each be switched independently — the reason homes are wired this way.

lessons.title: E.M.F., Internal Resistance and Maximum Power
lessons.notes_html:
The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy it supplies per unit charge; its unit is the volt. A real source also has internal resistance r, inside the source itself.

Terminal voltage V = E - I r

  • While the source delivers current, the terminal voltage is less than the e.m.f. (E is greater than V), because part of the energy is lost across r.
  • When no current is drawn (open circuit, I = 0), the terminal voltage equals the e.m.f. exactly — the only case in which V and E are the same (the ideal limit r = 0 gives it always).

Maximum Power Transfer

A source delivers maximum power to its load when the load resistance equals the internal resistance:

R = r

  • At this point only half of the total power reaches the load; the other half is wasted as heat inside the source, so the efficiency is 50%.

Worked Example: Terminal Voltage

A battery has an e.m.f. of 12.5 V and an internal resistance of 2.4 x 10-3 Ω. If the load current is 20 A, find the terminal voltage.

Step 1: Voltage lost inside the battery = I r = 20 x 2.4 x 10-3 = 0.048 V.

Step 2: V = E - I r = 12.5 - 0.048 = 12.45 V.

Answer: 12.45 V.

the energy it supplies per unit charge, measured in volts
mcqs.why: Electromotive force is the energy a source supplies per unit charge; a real source also has internal resistance r inside itself.

mcqs.why: With R = r, equal power is dissipated in the load and in the internal resistance, so the efficiency is 50%.

mcqs.why: V = E - I r: larger I means more energy lost across the internal resistance, so the terminal voltage falls.

mcqs.why: The terminal voltage is the e.m.f. minus the volts lost across the internal resistance: V = E - I r = 6 - 2 x 1 = 4 V.

mcqs.why: Maximum power transfer needs R = r = 1 ohm; the load then receives half the total power, the rest heating the source.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge and Potentiometer
lessons.notes_html:
Circuit Language

  • A node is a junction where two or more conductors meet and currents divide or combine. A node chosen as the zero-potential reference is called the datum node.
  • A loop is any closed conducting path in the circuit.

Kirchhoff's Laws

  • First law (junction rule): the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving it. It rests on the conservation of charge.
  • Second law (loop rule): around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of the potential drops. It rests on the conservation of energy.
  • Sign rules: passing through a source from its negative to its positive terminal, E is taken positive; passing through a resistor in the direction of the current, the potential decreases.

Wheatstone Bridge

Four resistors form a diamond, with a galvanometer joining the two middle points. The bridge is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer:

R1 / R2 = R3 / R4

  • With three known resistors, the fourth (unknown) follows from this condition. Being a null method, it is very accurate.

Potentiometer

A potentiometer measures potential difference and e.m.f. by the null method, drawing no current from the source being measured. A steady current through a uniform wire makes the potential fall uniformly along it; the unknown e.m.f. is balanced against a length of the wire at which the galvanometer shows no deflection. It is used to measure and compare e.m.f.s of cells, to find the internal resistance of a cell, and to calibrate voltmeters and ammeters.

Worked Example: E.M.F. by Potentiometer

The e.m.f. of a battery is balanced by 80 cm of potentiometer wire, while the 1.03 V e.m.f. of a standard cell is balanced by 55 cm. Find the e.m.f. of the battery.

Step 1: E.m.f. is proportional to the balancing length: E = 1.03 x (80 / 55).

Step 2: E = 1.03 x 1.4545 = 1.5 V.

Answer: 1.5 V.

Key Points

  • Coulomb's law: F = k Q1 Q2 / r2 with k = 9 x 109 N m2 C-2; the electron's charge is 1.6 x 10-19 C.
  • Field intensity E = F / q; field lines never cross and give the field direction by their tangent.
  • The field inside a conductor and inside a Faraday cage is zero.
  • Potential V = W / q is a scalar; E = -ΔV / Δd; 1 eV = 1.6 x 10-19 J.
  • A charge entering a uniform field at right angles follows a parabolic path.
  • Current is the drift of charge; in electrolytes and plasmas, ions of both signs carry it.
  • Ohm's law V = I R; resistance R = ρ L / A; conductivity is 1 / ρ.
  • Metals have a positive temperature coefficient; thermistors respond to heat and LDRs to light, both with falling resistance.
  • Series resistances add; parallel reciprocals add.
  • Terminal voltage V = E - I r; maximum power is transferred when R = r.
  • Kirchhoff's first law conserves charge, his second law conserves energy; the Wheatstone bridge balances at R1/R2 = R3/R4.

lessons.title: Magnetic Field of a Current-Carrying Conductor
lessons.notes_html:
A current-carrying conductor is surrounded by a magnetic field. The field lines around a long straight wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.

Right-Hand Grip Rule

Grip the conductor with the right hand, the thumb pointing along the current. The curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines circling the conductor.

Field Inside a Solenoid

A solenoid is a long coil of wire. Inside it the field is strong and nearly uniform, like the field of a bar magnet:

B = μ0 n I

  • μ0 — permeability of free space = 4π x 10-7 T m A-1
  • n — number of turns per unit length, I — current

Worked Example: Field Inside a Solenoid

A solenoid 10 cm long has 500 turns. Find the magnetic field inside it when it carries a current of 10 A.

Step 1: n = 500 / 0.10 = 5000 turns per metre.

Step 2: B = μ0 n I = 4π x 10-7 x 5000 x 10 = 4π x 10-7 x 5 x 104.

Answer: B = 6.28 x 10-2 T.

lessons.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
lessons.notes_html:
A conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a magnetic force, because the field acts on each of its drifting charge carriers:

F = B I L sin θ

  • B — flux density, I — current, L — length of conductor in the field, θ — angle between the conductor and the field
  • The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field (θ = 90°) and zero when it is parallel to the field.
  • Its direction is perpendicular to both the field and the conductor, given by Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger Field, second finger Current, thumb Motion (force).

The formula comes from adding the forces q v B sin θ on all the carriers in the length L: with n carriers per unit volume in a wire of cross-section A, the total is F = (n A L) q v B sin θ, and since I = n A q v, this is F = B I L sin θ.

Worked Example: Force on a Conductor

A conductor of length 20 cm carrying a current of 10 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 2 T, its length at 60° to the field. Calculate the force on the conductor.

Step 1: F = B I L sin θ = 2 x 10 x 0.20 x sin 60°.

Step 2: sin 60° = 0.866, so F = 4 x 0.866 = 3.46 N.

Answer: F = 3.5 N (approximately).

mcqs.q: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor in a field is
options: F = B I L sin theta
F = B I L cos theta

mcqs.why: F = B I L sin theta, where L is the length of conductor in the field and theta the angle between the conductor and the field.

mcqs.q: The force on a conductor is greatest when the conductor is
options: at right angles to the field (theta = 90 degrees)
mcqs.why: F = B I L sin theta is greatest at theta = 90 degrees (sin = 1) and zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

mcqs.q: The force on a conductor parallel to the field is
mcqs.why: At theta = 0, sin theta = 0, so F = B I L sin theta = 0 for a conductor parallel to the field.

options: the field, with the thumb along the current
the current, with the thumb along the field
the motion (force), with first finger Field and second finger Current
mcqs.why: Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger Field, second finger Current, thumb Motion (force); the force is perpendicular to both field and conductor.

mcqs.q: A 20 cm conductor carrying 10 A sits at 60 degrees in a 2 T field. The force on it is about
mcqs.why: F = B I L sin theta = 2 x 10 x 0.20 x sin 60 = 4 x 0.866 = 3.46 N, about 3.5 N.

mcqs.q: The formula F = B I L sin theta comes from adding the forces on
options: all the drifting charge carriers in the length L, each feeling q v B sin theta, with I = n A q v
the electrons in the whole circuit
the field lines crossing the wire
mcqs.why: Total force = (n A L) q v B sin theta for n carriers per unit volume in cross-section A; since I = n A q v, this is F = B I L sin theta.

mcqs.q: A conductor experiences a magnetic force because the field acts on
options: the conductor as a magnet only if it is iron
each of its drifting charge carriers
mcqs.why: A conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force because the field acts on each of its drifting charge carriers.

mcqs.q: A 0.5 m conductor at right angles to a 0.4 T field carries 5 A. The force on it is
mcqs.why: At right angles sin theta = 1, so F = B I L sin 90 = 0.4 x 5 x 0.5 x 1 = 1 N.

mcqs.q: Reversing the current in a conductor in a magnetic field
options: reverses the direction of the force on it
mcqs.why: By Fleming's left-hand rule, reversing the current (second finger) reverses the force (thumb), while the magnitude B I L sin theta is unchanged.

mcqs.q: The force on a current-carrying conductor is perpendicular to
options: both the magnetic field and the conductor
neither; it acts along the current
mcqs.why: Its direction is perpendicular to both the field and the conductor, as Fleming's left-hand rule arranges the three mutually perpendicular directions.

lessons.title: Force on a Moving Charged Particle
lessons.notes_html:
A single charged particle moving in a magnetic field experiences the force:

F = q v B sin θ

  • The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the particle's direction but never its speed or kinetic energy — a magnetic field does no work on a moving charge.
  • Moving parallel to the field (θ = 0°): no force at all, the particle continues straight.
  • Moving perpendicular to the field (θ = 90°): the force acts as a centripetal force and the particle moves in a circle:

r = m v / (q B)

  • A proton (positive) is deflected in the direction of v x B by Fleming's left-hand rule; an electron (negative) is deflected the opposite way.

Worked Example: Force on a Proton

A proton enters a magnetic field of flux density 1.5 Wb m-2 with a velocity of 2 x 107 m s-1 at an angle of 45° with the field. Compute the force on the proton. (Charge on a proton = 1.6 x 10-19 C.)

Step 1: F = q v B sin θ = 1.6 x 10-19 x 2 x 107 x 1.5 x sin 45°.

Step 2: sin 45° = 0.707, so F = 4.8 x 10-12 x 0.707.

Answer: F = 3.4 x 10-12 N.

Worked Example: Speed of an Electron (Check the Data!)

An electron moves at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.2 T and experiences a force of 2 x 10-2 N. What is its speed?

Step 1: v = F / (e B) = 2 x 10-2 / (1.6 x 10-19 x 0.2) = 2 x 10-2 / 3.2 x 10-20.

Answer: 6.25 x 1017 m s-1 by the arithmetic — but this is faster than the speed of light (3 x 108 m s-1), so the printed data in the book are unphysical; no real electron can reach this speed.

mcqs.q: The force on a single charged particle moving in a magnetic field is
options: F = B I L sin theta for one particle
F = q v B sin theta
F = q v B cos theta
mcqs.why: A charged particle moving in a field feels F = q v B sin theta, always perpendicular to its velocity.

mcqs.q: Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it
options: changes the particle's direction but never its speed or kinetic energy — a magnetic field does no work on a moving charge
mcqs.why: A force perpendicular to the motion does no work: the magnetic force changes direction only, never speed or kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: A charged particle moving parallel to the field (theta = 0) experiences
options: a force opposite to its motion
no force at all, and continues straight
mcqs.why: At theta = 0, sin theta = 0, so F = q v B sin theta = 0: the particle continues straight.

mcqs.q: A charged particle moving perpendicular to the field moves in a circle of radius
mcqs.why: The force acts as a centripetal force: q v B = m v^2 / r, so r = m v / (q B).

mcqs.q: A proton enters a 1.5 T field at 2 x 10^7 m s-1 at 45 degrees. The force on it is
An electron in a magnetic field is deflected
options: the same way as a proton
not at all, being too light
opposite to the direction a proton would be deflected, because its charge is negative
mcqs.why: A proton (positive) is deflected in the direction of v x B by Fleming's left-hand rule; an electron (negative) is deflected the opposite way.

mcqs.q: An electron at right angles to a 0.2 T field feels a force of 2 x 10^-2 N. The formal speed F / (e B) is 6.25 x 10^17 m s-1, which shows that
options: electrons can travel faster than light
the printed data are unphysical, since this exceeds the speed of light (3 x 10^8 m s-1) and no real electron can reach it
mcqs.why: v = F / (e B) = 2 x 10^-2 / (1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.2) = 6.25 x 10^17 m s-1 — faster than light, so the book's printed data are unphysical, as the notes point out.

mcqs.q: Doubling the speed of a charged particle in a perpendicular field doubles
options: both the force (F = q v B) and the radius of its circular path (r = m v / (q B))
mcqs.why: F = q v B is proportional to v, and r = m v / (q B) is also proportional to v, so doubling v doubles both.

mcqs.q: A proton of mass 1.67 x 10^-27 kg moves at 1 x 10^6 m s-1 perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. Its path radius is about
In a circle in a magnetic field, the particle's kinetic energy
options: stays constant, because the force does no work
mcqs.why: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed and kinetic energy stay constant while the direction changes.

lessons.title: Magnetic Flux and Magnetic Flux Density
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic flux Φ is the total number of magnetic field lines passing through a surface:

Φ = B A cos θ

  • A — area of the surface, θ — angle between the field and the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface)
  • Flux is maximum when the field is perpendicular to the plane of the area, that is parallel to its normal (θ = 0°, cos θ = 1): Φ = B A.
  • Flux is minimum (zero) when the field lies in the plane of the area (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0).
  • SI unit of flux: the weber (Wb).

Magnetic flux density B is the flux per unit area held normal to the field — it is the strength of the magnetic field itself:

B = Φ / A

  • SI unit: the tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 Wb m-2. In base units, 1 tesla = 1 kg s-2 A-1.
  • The unit of induced e.m.f. is the volt.

mcqs.q: Magnetic flux through a surface is defined as
options: Phi = B A sin theta in all conventions
Phi = B A cos theta, where theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface
mcqs.why: Flux is the total number of field lines through a surface: Phi = B A cos theta, with theta measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface).

mcqs.q: Flux is maximum when
options: the field lies in the plane of the area
the field is perpendicular to the plane of the area, i.e. parallel to its normal (theta = 0, cos theta = 1): Phi = B A
mcqs.why: With the field along the normal, cos theta = 1 and Phi = B A, the maximum; flux is zero when the field lies in the plane (theta = 90).

mcqs.q: Flux is zero when
options: the field lies in the plane of the area (theta = 90 degrees, cos theta = 0)
the field is perpendicular to the area
mcqs.why: Field in the plane of the area means no lines pass through it: theta = 90 degrees from the normal, cos theta = 0, so Phi = 0.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is
mcqs.why: SI unit of flux: the weber (Wb). Flux density is measured in tesla, 1 T = 1 Wb m-2.

mcqs.q: Magnetic flux density B is
options: the total flux through any surface
the flux multiplied by the area
the flux per unit area held normal to the field, B = Phi / A — the strength of the field itself
mcqs.why: B = Phi / A for area held normal to the field; its unit is the tesla, 1 T = 1 Wb m-2 = 1 kg s-2 A-1 in base units.

mcqs.q: One tesla equals
mcqs.why: 1 T = 1 Wb m-2: a flux of one weber through one square metre held normal to the field.

mcqs.q: A field of 0.5 T passes perpendicular through an area of 0.02 m^2. The flux is
mcqs.why: With the field perpendicular to the area, theta = 0 and cos theta = 1: Phi = B A cos 0 = 0.5 x 0.02 x 1 = 0.01 Wb.

mcqs.q: The same field and area, with the field at 60 degrees to the normal, give flux
mcqs.why: Phi = B A cos theta = 0.5 x 0.02 x cos 60 = 0.01 x 0.5 = 0.005 Wb.

mcqs.q: In base units, 1 tesla equals
mcqs.why: The notes give 1 tesla = 1 kg s-2 A-1 in base units (equivalently 1 Wb m-2 or 1 N A-1 m-1).

mcqs.q: Flux density is also called
options: the strength of the magnetic field itself (the B-field)
mcqs.why: Magnetic flux density B is the flux per unit area normal to the field — it is the strength of the magnetic field itself.

lessons.title: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law
lessons.notes_html:
An induced e.m.f. is the e.m.f. generated in a circuit by a change in the magnetic flux linked with it. Experiments show it clearly: pushing a bar magnet into a coil deflects a galvanometer (and pulling it out deflects it the other way); moving the coil instead of the magnet works just as well; changing the current in a neighbouring coil induces an e.m.f. too; and rotating a coil in a field — the generator — gives a continuously varying e.m.f. In every case the e.m.f. appears only while the flux is changing: a coil and magnet closed together but at rest give zero induced e.m.f.

Faraday's Law (given by Faraday)

ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt

  • The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage; N is the number of turns.

Lenz's Law and the Negative Sign

The negative sign is Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. and current always act in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced them. If the flux increases, the induced current makes a field opposing the increase; if the flux decreases, it makes a field supporting it. Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy: the electrical energy produced comes from the mechanical work done against this opposition.

Induced E.M.F. versus Induced Current

  • Induced e.m.f. is the cause: the voltage generated by the changing flux. It exists even in an open circuit, as a potential difference across the ends.
  • Induced current is the effect: it flows only when the circuit is closed and the e.m.f. can drive charge around it.

Worked Example: E.M.F. When the Flux Reverses

A coil of 200 turns is linked by a flux of 40 mWb. If this flux is reversed in 4 ms, determine the average induced e.m.f. in the coil.

Step 1: Reversing the flux changes it from +40 mWb to -40 mWb, so ΔΦ = 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb.

Step 2: ε = N ΔΦ / Δt = 200 x 0.08 / 0.004 = 200 x 20.

Answer: 4000 V. (Note: the book prints 2000 V, which is the answer for the flux merely falling to zero; for a full reversal the change is doubled, giving 4000 V.)

mcqs.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced e.m.f. is
options: epsilon = N Phi, proportional to the flux itself
epsilon = - N delta Phi / delta t: proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage
mcqs.why: The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage; N is the number of turns.

mcqs.q: The negative sign in Faraday's law expresses Lenz's law, which says the induced e.m.f. and current
options: always act in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced them
always aid the change in flux
flow in the direction of the flux
mcqs.why: If the flux increases, the induced current makes a field opposing the increase; if it decreases, a field supporting it. Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy.

mcqs.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of
options: the conservation of energy: the electrical energy produced comes from the mechanical work done against the opposition
mcqs.why: The work done pushing against the induced opposition is exactly the electrical energy produced — Lenz's law is energy conservation in induction.

mcqs.q: An induced e.m.f. appears only while
options: a magnet is near the coil, moving or not
the flux is changing; a coil and magnet at rest together give zero induced e.m.f.
the flux is large and steady
mcqs.why: Pushing a magnet in or out, moving the coil, changing a neighbouring current, or rotating a coil all work — in every case the e.m.f. appears only while the flux changes.

mcqs.q: Induced e.m.f. differs from induced current in that the e.m.f.
options: flows only in a closed circuit
is the effect of the current
is the cause: it exists even in an open circuit, while current flows only when the circuit is closed
mcqs.why: Induced e.m.f. is the voltage generated by the changing flux and exists as a p.d. across open ends; induced current is the effect, flowing only in a closed circuit.

mcqs.q: A coil of 200 turns is linked by a flux of 40 mWb, which is reversed in 4 ms. The average induced e.m.f. is
mcqs.why: Reversing changes the flux from +40 to -40 mWb, so delta Phi = 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb. epsilon = N delta Phi / delta t = 200 x 0.08 / 0.004 = 4000 V. (The book prints 2000 V, the value for flux falling only to zero.)

mcqs.q: If the same flux merely fell to zero in 4 ms, the induced e.m.f. would be
mcqs.why: delta Phi = 40 mWb = 0.04 Wb. epsilon = 200 x 0.04 / 0.004 = 200 x 10 = 2000 V — half the reversal value.

mcqs.q: Doubling the number of turns on a coil (same flux change) makes the induced e.m.f.
options: double, since epsilon is proportional to N
mcqs.why: epsilon = - N delta Phi / delta t is proportional to N, the number of turns linked by the changing flux.

mcqs.q: A rotating coil in a magnetic field — the generator — produces
options: an e.m.f. only when the coil stops
no e.m.f. because the field is steady
a continuously varying e.m.f., because the flux through the coil changes continuously
mcqs.why: Rotation changes the flux linkage continuously (through the changing angle), giving a continuously varying — alternating — e.m.f.

mcqs.q: Changing the current in a neighbouring coil induces an e.m.f. in a coil because
options: the changing current changes the flux linking the coil
the coils are connected by wire
the first coil heats the second
mcqs.why: A changing current in a neighbouring coil changes its field and hence the flux through the second coil — mutual induction, one of the demonstrated cases.

lessons.title: Mutual Induction and Self-Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Mutual Induction

Mutual induction is the production of an e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil, through the changing flux that links them:

ε = - M ΔI / Δt

  • M — coefficient of mutual induction (mutual inductance): the e.m.f. induced in the second coil per unit rate of change of current in the first.

Self-Induction

Self-induction is the production of an e.m.f. in a coil by the change of its own current, as its own flux changes:

ε = - L ΔI / Δt

  • L — self-inductance of the coil. By Lenz's law the self-induced e.m.f. opposes the change: it delays the growth of current at switch-on and its decay at switch-off, which is why breaking an inductive circuit produces a spark.

The Henry

One henry (H) is the inductance of a coil in which an e.m.f. of 1 volt is induced when the current changes at 1 ampere per second: 1 H = 1 V s A-1 = 1 Wb A-1. Its dimensions are [M L2 T-2 A-2].

Worked Example: Mutual Inductance

When the current in coil A is increased uniformly from zero to 18 A in 0.3 s, an e.m.f. of 6 V is induced in a nearby coil B. Find the mutual inductance between the coils.

Step 1: Rate of change of current = 18 / 0.3 = 60 A s-1.

Step 2: M = ε / (ΔI / Δt) = 6 / 60 = 0.1 H.

Answer: M = 0.1 H.

Worked Example: Self-Inductance

The current in a coil changes by 3 A in 60 ms, and an e.m.f. of 10 V is induced in the coil. What is its self-inductance?

Step 1: Rate of change of current = 3 / 0.060 = 50 A s-1.

Step 2: L = ε / (ΔI / Δt) = 10 / 50 = 0.2 H.

Answer: L = 0.2 H.

mcqs.q: Mutual induction is
options: the production of an e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a neighbouring coil, through the changing flux that links them
a coil inducing an e.m.f. in itself
the heating of a coil by its own current
mcqs.why: Mutual induction: epsilon = - M delta I / delta t, where M is the coefficient of mutual induction between the two coils.

mcqs.q: The coefficient of mutual induction M is defined as
options: the e.m.f. induced in the second coil per unit rate of change of current in the first
the product of the two currents
mcqs.why: M is the e.m.f. induced in the second coil per unit rate of change of current in the first, measured in henrys.

mcqs.q: Self-induction is
options: an e.m.f. from a neighbouring coil
the production of an e.m.f. in a coil by the change of its own current, as its own flux changes: epsilon = - L delta I / delta t
the heating effect of a current
mcqs.why: Self-induction: the coil's own changing current changes its own flux and induces an e.m.f. opposing the change, with L the self-inductance.

mcqs.q: One henry is the inductance of a coil in which
options: a current of 1 A always flows
a flux of 1 Wb is stored permanently
an e.m.f. of 1 volt is induced when the current changes at 1 ampere per second: 1 H = 1 V s A-1
mcqs.why: 1 H = 1 V s A-1 = 1 Wb A-1: the inductance giving 1 V of induced e.m.f. for a current change of 1 A per second.

mcqs.q: The current in coil A rises uniformly from 0 to 18 A in 0.3 s, inducing 6 V in coil B. The mutual inductance is
mcqs.why: Rate of change of current = 18 / 0.3 = 60 A s-1. M = epsilon / (delta I / delta t) = 6 / 60 = 0.1 H.

mcqs.q: A coil's current changes by 3 A in 60 ms, inducing 10 V in itself. Its self-inductance is
mcqs.why: Rate of change = 3 / 0.060 = 50 A s-1. L = epsilon / (delta I / delta t) = 10 / 50 = 0.2 H.

mcqs.q: The self-induced e.m.f. delays the growth of current at switch-on and its decay at switch-off because, by Lenz's law, it
options: opposes the change of current producing it
mcqs.why: By Lenz's law the self-induced e.m.f. opposes the change: it delays growth at switch-on and decay at switch-off, which is why breaking an inductive circuit produces a spark.

mcqs.q: Breaking an inductive circuit produces a spark because
options: air becomes a conductor when hot only
the rapidly collapsing current induces a large e.m.f. opposing the decay
mcqs.why: At switch-off the current tries to collapse quickly; the self-induced e.m.f. opposing the decay is large (L times a large rate of change) and can spark across the gap.

mcqs.q: The dimensions of inductance (the henry) are
mcqs.why: From epsilon = L delta I / delta t, L = (energy per charge) x time / current, giving dimensions [M L2 T-2 A-2] as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: If the current in a coil changes twice as fast, the self-induced e.m.f.
options: doubles, since epsilon = L x (rate of change of current)
mcqs.why: epsilon = - L delta I / delta t is proportional to the rate of change of current, so doubling the rate doubles the e.m.f.

lessons.title: The Transformer
lessons.notes_html:
A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating supply. It works on mutual induction: an alternating current in the primary coil produces a continuously changing flux in the laminated soft-iron core, and this changing flux links the secondary coil and induces an alternating e.m.f. in it. The soft iron core enhances the magnetic flux and guides it from one coil to the other. A transformer works only with A.C., because a steady current produces no changing flux.

Vs / Vp = Ns / Np

  • Step-up transformer: Ns greater than Np, so the voltage rises and the current falls. Used at power stations so electricity can be transmitted at high voltage.
  • Step-down transformer: Ns less than Np, so the voltage falls and the current rises. Used near consumers to deliver safe voltages such as 220 V.
  • An ideal transformer wastes nothing: input power = output power.
  • For long-distance transmission we use a smaller current and a higher voltage, because the heating loss in the lines is I2 R and falls rapidly as the current is reduced.

Power Losses in a Real Transformer

  • Copper losses: I2 R heating in the windings.
  • Eddy current losses: circulating currents induced in the core — reduced by laminating the core.
  • Hysteresis losses: energy lost in repeatedly magnetizing and demagnetizing the core — reduced by using soft iron.
  • Flux leakage: flux that links only one coil — reduced by winding the coils close together on the same core.

Worked Example: Turns on a Step-Down Transformer

A step-down transformer is used on a 1 kV line to deliver 220 V. How many turns are on the primary winding if the secondary has 50 turns?

Step 1: Np / Ns = Vp / Vs, so Np = 50 x (1000 / 220).

Step 2: Np = 50 x 4.545 = 227.3.

Answer: about 227 turns on the primary.

Key Points

  • The field around a straight current is concentric circles; find its direction with the right-hand grip rule.
  • Force on a conductor: F = B I L sin θ, direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
  • Force on a moving charge: F = q v B sin θ; it does no work, and a charge crossing the field at right angles moves in a circle of radius m v / (q B).
  • Flux Φ = B A cos θ (unit weber); flux density B = Φ / A (unit tesla).
  • Faraday's law: ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt; the negative sign is Lenz's law, which follows from conservation of energy.
  • Induced e.m.f. exists in an open circuit; induced current needs a closed circuit.
  • Mutual inductance M and self-inductance L are both measured in henries.
  • A transformer works on mutual induction with A.C. only: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.
  • Transmit power at high voltage and low current to cut I2 R losses.

mcqs.q: A transformer works on the principle of
options: mutual induction: an alternating current in the primary produces a continuously changing flux in the core, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary
mcqs.why: The laminated soft-iron core carries the changing flux from primary to secondary; the changing flux links the secondary and induces its e.m.f.

mcqs.q: A transformer works only with A.C. because
options: the core would melt with D.C. instantly
a steady (D.C.) current produces no changing flux, so no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary
mcqs.why: Induction needs changing flux; a steady current's flux is constant, so a transformer works only with alternating current.

mcqs.q: The transformer equation relating voltages and turns is
options: Vs x Vp = Ns x Np
mcqs.why: The induced e.m.f. per turn is the same for both coils, so the voltages are in the same ratio as the turns: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.

mcqs.q: In a step-up transformer,
options: Ns is greater than Np, so the voltage rises and the current falls; used at power stations for transmission
Ns is less than Np and the voltage falls
mcqs.why: Step-up: more secondary turns raise the voltage and lower the current, used at power stations so electricity can be transmitted at high voltage.

mcqs.q: In a step-down transformer,
options: Ns is less than Np, so the voltage falls and the current rises; used near consumers to deliver safe voltages such as 220 V
the voltage rises and current falls
mcqs.why: Step-down transformers near consumers reduce the transmission voltage to safe values such as 220 V; the current rises correspondingly.

mcqs.q: A step-down transformer on a 1 kV line delivers 220 V; its secondary has 50 turns. The primary has about
mcqs.why: Np / Ns = Vp / Vs, so Np = 50 x (1000 / 220) = 50 x 4.545 = 227.3, about 227 turns.

mcqs.q: For long-distance transmission, high voltage and small current are used because
options: energy is created by stepping up
the heating loss in the lines is I^2 R and falls rapidly as the current is reduced
mcqs.why: Line loss is I^2 R heating: halving the current quarters the loss, so transmitting at high voltage (small current) is far more efficient.

mcqs.q: Eddy current losses in a transformer core are reduced by
mcqs.why: Circulating eddy currents induced in the core are reduced by laminating the core into insulated sheets.

mcqs.q: Hysteresis losses are reduced by
options: using soft iron for the core, which magnetizes and demagnetizes easily
mcqs.why: Hysteresis loss is energy lost in repeatedly magnetizing and demagnetizing the core — reduced by using soft iron. Lamination reduces eddy currents instead.

mcqs.q: An ideal transformer wastes nothing, so
options: both voltage and current rise together
input power equals output power: Vp Ip = Vs Is
no current flows in the primary
mcqs.why: An ideal transformer wastes nothing: input power = output power, which is why stepping voltage up steps the current down in the same ratio.

lessons.title: Relative Motion and Frames of Reference
lessons.notes_html:
Relative motion is the motion of a body as observed from a particular frame of reference: the same motion looks different to different observers.

  • A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest for a fellow passenger, but in motion for an observer standing on the platform.
  • Raindrops fall vertically, yet appear to fall slanting to a person walking through the rain.
  • Two cars moving in the same direction at the same speed are at rest relative to each other, while a car coming the opposite way appears to move with the sum of the two speeds.

Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames

  • An inertial frame is at rest or moving with uniform velocity (no acceleration). Newton's laws hold in it in their simple form.
  • A non-inertial frame is accelerated or rotating. In it, fictitious forces such as centrifugal force appear, and Newton's laws need correction terms.

mcqs.q: Relative motion is
options: always the motion relative to the ground
the motion of the observer only
the motion of a body as observed from a particular frame of reference: the same motion looks different to different observers
motion at the speed of light
mcqs.why: A passenger in a moving train is at rest for a fellow passenger but in motion for an observer on the platform — motion is relative to the frame of reference.

mcqs.q: A passenger sitting in a moving train is
options: at rest only if the train is slow
at rest for a fellow passenger, but in motion for an observer standing on the platform
mcqs.why: The same body can be at rest in one frame and moving in another; that is the meaning of relative motion.

mcqs.q: Raindrops fall vertically, yet appear to fall slanting to a person walking through the rain because
options: the observed motion is relative to the walker's frame of reference
the wind always blows the rain
mcqs.why: Combining the rain's vertical fall with the walker's horizontal motion gives a slanting apparent path in the walker's frame.

mcqs.q: Two cars moving in the same direction at the same speed are
options: moving at twice the speed relative to each other
at rest relative to each other
in motion relative to each other at their common speed
mcqs.why: With equal velocities, their relative velocity is zero: they are at rest relative to each other.

mcqs.q: A car coming the opposite way appears to move with
options: the difference of the two speeds
the sum of the two speeds
mcqs.why: For opposite directions the speeds add in the relative frame: the oncoming car appears to move with the sum of the two speeds.

mcqs.q: An inertial frame is one that
options: is attached to the Earth in all cases
is at rest or moving with uniform velocity (no acceleration), so Newton's laws hold in it in their simple form
mcqs.why: Inertial frames have no acceleration; Newton's laws hold in them in their simple form.

mcqs.q: A non-inertial frame is
options: an accelerated or rotating frame, in which fictitious forces such as centrifugal force appear and Newton's laws need correction terms
a frame moving at uniform velocity
a frame in which Newton's laws hold simply
mcqs.why: In non-inertial frames, fictitious forces such as centrifugal force appear, and Newton's laws need correction terms.

options: appears only in a rotating (non-inertial) frame, not in an inertial one
mcqs.why: Fictitious forces such as centrifugal force appear in accelerated or rotating frames; in an inertial frame they are absent and Newton's laws hold simply.

mcqs.q: A car moving at 60 km h-1 meets one coming the other way at 40 km h-1. The second car appears to approach at
mcqs.why: Opposite directions: the apparent speed is the sum, 60 + 40 = 100 km h-1, in the first car's frame.
