lessons.title: Special Theory of Relativity
lessons.notes_html:
Einstein's special theory of relativity (1905) rests on two postulates:

  • All the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference.
  • The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.

Its Main Consequences

  • Relativity of simultaneity: events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.
  • Length contraction: a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion:

L = L0 √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Time dilation: a moving clock runs slow:

T = T0 / √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Mass variation: the mass of a moving object increases:

m = m0 / √(1 - v2 / c2)

  • Mass-energy equivalence:

E = m c2

E0 = m0 c2

  • E0 — rest energy of a body of rest mass m0
  • Space-time is described with four coordinates, the fourth being x4 = i c t.
  • A particle can travel at the speed of light only if its rest mass is zero, like the photon: for any massive particle the mass would become infinite at v = c, needing infinite energy, so massive particles always stay below c.

mcqs.q: Einstein's special theory of relativity (1905) rests on two postulates, the first being that
options: the speed of light depends on the observer
Newton's laws fail in moving frames
time is absolute for all observers
all the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
mcqs.why: First postulate: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Second: the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers.

mcqs.q: The second postulate of special relativity states that
options: the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer
light slows down when the source moves away
light speeds up when the observer approaches
the speed of light is relative like other speeds
mcqs.why: The constancy of c for all observers, whatever the motion of source or observer, is the second postulate and leads to length contraction and time dilation.

mcqs.q: Length contraction is given by
options: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2): a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion
L = L0 (1 - v / c) always exactly
mcqs.why: A moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2), always less than the rest length L0.

mcqs.q: Time dilation is given by
options: T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2): a moving clock runs slow
mcqs.why: A moving clock runs slow: the moving observer measures a longer period T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) than the proper period T0.

mcqs.q: The mass of a moving object
options: decreases: m = m0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)
stays exactly m0 at all speeds
increases: m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)
mcqs.why: Mass variation: m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2), growing without limit as v approaches c.

mcqs.q: Mass-energy equivalence is expressed by
options: E = m c^2, with rest energy E0 = m0 c^2
E = (1/2) m c^2 for rest energy
mcqs.why: E = m c^2; a body at rest still has rest energy E0 = m0 c^2 locked in its mass.

mcqs.q: Relativity of simultaneity means that
options: all observers agree on which events are simultaneous
events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another
mcqs.why: One consequence of the postulates: simultaneity is relative — events simultaneous in one inertial frame need not be simultaneous in another.

mcqs.q: A particle can travel at the speed of light only if
options: it is accelerated for long enough
its rest mass is zero, like the photon; a massive particle's mass would become infinite at v = c, needing infinite energy
it is a particle of antimatter
mcqs.why: At v = c the factor 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) becomes infinite, so massive particles always stay below c; only zero-rest-mass particles like the photon travel at c.

mcqs.q: Space-time is described with four coordinates, the fourth being
mcqs.why: Space-time uses four coordinates, the fourth being x4 = i c t, mixing time with the three space coordinates.

mcqs.q: The rest energy of a body of rest mass 1 kg is
mcqs.why: E0 = m0 c^2 = 1 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 9 x 10^16 J — the huge energy locked in even 1 kg of mass.

lessons.title: Relativistic Effects: Worked Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Length Contraction

How fast must a rocket go for its length to be contracted to 80% of its rest length?

Step 1: L / L0 = 0.80 = √(1 - v2 / c2). Squaring: 0.64 = 1 - v2 / c2.

Step 2: v2 / c2 = 1 - 0.64 = 0.36, so v = 0.6 c.

Answer: v = 0.6 x 3 x 108 = 1.8 x 108 m s-1.

Worked Example: Time Dilation

The period of a seconds pendulum is 2 s in its own frame. What period does an observer measure who moves at 0.9 c relative to the pendulum's frame?

Step 1: T = T0 / √(1 - v2 / c2) = 2 / √(1 - 0.81) = 2 / √0.19.

Step 2: √0.19 = 0.436, so T = 2 / 0.436 = 4.6 s.

Answer: 4.6 s — the moving observer sees the pendulum swinging more slowly.

Worked Example: Relativistic Mass

Calculate the mass of an object of rest mass m0 moving at 0.85 c.

Step 1: m = m0 / √(1 - 0.852) = m0 / √(1 - 0.7225) = m0 / √0.2775.

Step 2: √0.2775 = 0.527, so m = m0 / 0.527.

Answer: m = 1.9 m0 — the mass is nearly doubled.

options: only along its direction of motion
not at all below 0.5 c in principle
mcqs.why: The notes specify: a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion; the perpendicular dimensions are unchanged.

mcqs.q: A clock moving at 0.6 c ticks 10 s in its own frame. A stationary observer measures the interval as
mcqs.why: T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 10 / 0.8 = 12.5 s: the moving clock runs slow, so the observer measures a longer interval.

mcqs.q: At ordinary everyday speeds, relativistic effects are
options: negligibly small, because v^2 / c^2 is tiny and the factor is nearly 1
mcqs.why: For v far below c, sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) is nearly 1, so lengths, times and masses are barely affected — relativity matters near light speed.

mcqs.q: The relativistic mass formula shows that reaching c would require infinite energy because
options: the fuel would run out first
m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) grows without limit as v approaches c
mcqs.why: As v approaches c the denominator approaches zero and the mass grows without limit, needing infinite energy — so massive particles always stay below c.

lessons.title: Discovery of the Fundamental Particles and Accelerators
lessons.notes_html:
A Brief History

  • 1897: the electron, discovered by Thomson — the first fundamental particle.
  • 1917: the proton, identified by Rutherford.
  • 1932: the neutron (Chadwick), and the positron — the first antiparticle discovered (the antielectron), predicted by Dirac and found by Anderson in cosmic rays.
  • Cosmic-ray studies then revealed the muon, the pion and the kaons.
  • 1964: the quark model of Gell-Mann and Zweig explained hadrons as combinations of quarks.
  • 1983: the W and Z bosons found at CERN; 1995: the top quark; 2012: the Higgs boson, completing the Standard Model's particle list.

Cosmic Rays

Cosmic rays are highly energetic particles — mostly protons and atomic nuclei — arriving at the Earth from outer space. Their sources are violent events: the Sun, supernova explosions in our galaxy, and still more energetic sources beyond it such as active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts. Entering the atmosphere, they collide with air nuclei and produce showers of secondary particles.

Particle Accelerators

A particle accelerator accelerates charged particles to very high speeds and energies with electric fields, while magnetic fields steer and focus the beam. Types include linear accelerators and circular machines (cyclotrons, synchrotrons and the Large Hadron Collider). Their uses:

  • Probing the structure of matter and discovering new particles.
  • Producing radioisotopes for medical diagnosis and cancer therapy.
  • Materials testing and sterilization.
  • Industrial uses such as ion implantation in semiconductors.

mcqs.q: The first fundamental particle discovered was
options: the electron, discovered by Thomson in 1897
mcqs.why: 1897: the electron, discovered by Thomson — the first fundamental particle. The proton followed (Rutherford, 1917) and the neutron (Chadwick, 1932).

mcqs.q: The proton was identified by
mcqs.why: 1917: the proton, identified by Rutherford. Thomson found the electron (1897); Chadwick the neutron (1932).

mcqs.q: The neutron was discovered by
mcqs.why: 1932: the neutron (Chadwick), and in the same year the positron — the first antiparticle discovered.

mcqs.q: The positron, the first antiparticle discovered, was
options: predicted by Dirac and found by Anderson in cosmic rays in 1932
found by Thomson in cathode rays
mcqs.why: The positron (antielectron) was predicted by Dirac and found by Anderson in cosmic rays in 1932.

mcqs.q: The quark model, explaining hadrons as combinations of quarks, was proposed by
mcqs.why: 1964: the quark model of Gell-Mann and Zweig explained hadrons as combinations of quarks.

mcqs.q: The Higgs boson, completing the Standard Model's particle list, was found in
mcqs.why: 1983: W and Z bosons at CERN; 1995: the top quark; 2012: the Higgs boson, completing the Standard Model's particle list.

mcqs.q: Cosmic rays are
options: electromagnetic waves from the Sun only
highly energetic particles — mostly protons and atomic nuclei — arriving at the Earth from outer space
mcqs.why: Cosmic rays come from violent sources: the Sun, supernovae, active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts; entering the atmosphere they produce showers of secondary particles.

mcqs.q: In a particle accelerator, charged particles are accelerated to high energies by
options: electric fields, while magnetic fields steer and focus the beam
magnetic fields, while electric fields steer
mcqs.why: Accelerators use electric fields to accelerate and magnetic fields to steer and focus; types include linear accelerators and circular machines such as the LHC.

mcqs.q: The Large Hadron Collider is an example of
options: a circular particle accelerator (a synchrotron-type machine)
mcqs.why: Circular machines include cyclotrons, synchrotrons and the Large Hadron Collider; accelerators also produce medical radioisotopes and are used in industry.

mcqs.q: Besides probing matter and discovering particles, accelerators are used for
options: producing radioisotopes for medical diagnosis and cancer therapy, materials testing, sterilization and ion implantation in semiconductors
mcqs.why: The listed uses: probing matter, discovering particles, medical radioisotopes and cancer therapy, materials testing and sterilization, and ion implantation in semiconductors.

lessons.title: Particles and Antiparticles
lessons.notes_html:
Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and lifetime but opposite charge and opposite values of the other additive quantum numbers (baryon number, lepton number and so on).

  • Electron and positron (antielectron) — the first antiparticle discovered.
  • Proton and antiproton; neutron and antineutron.
  • When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate each other and their mass appears as gamma-ray photons.

Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry

The universe contains far more matter than antimatter, although the Big Bang should have made them in equal amounts. This baryon asymmetry — an imbalance in the number of baryons — is an unsolved mystery: the known CP violation in weak interactions is far too small to explain it, so some process in the very early universe must have favoured matter by about one part in a billion. The surviving excess is all the matter we see; the rest annihilated into radiation.

mcqs.q: An antiparticle has, compared with its particle,
options: double the mass and opposite charge
the same charge but opposite mass
the same mass and lifetime but opposite charge and opposite values of the other additive quantum numbers
mcqs.why: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and lifetime but opposite charge and opposite baryon number, lepton number and so on.

mcqs.q: The antiparticle of the electron is
options: the positron (antielectron) — the first antiparticle discovered
mcqs.why: Electron and positron (antielectron) head the list of particle-antiparticle pairs; the positron was the first antiparticle discovered.

mcqs.q: When a particle meets its antiparticle,
options: they annihilate each other and their mass appears as gamma-ray photons
mcqs.why: Particle + antiparticle annihilate, converting their mass into gamma-ray photons (E = m c^2 for both masses).

mcqs.q: The matter-antimatter asymmetry (baryon asymmetry) is the puzzle that
options: antimatter is slightly heavier than matter
the universe contains far more matter than antimatter, although the Big Bang should have made them in equal amounts
matter and antimatter have different charges
mcqs.why: The surviving excess of matter — favoured by about one part in a billion in the early universe — is all the matter we see; the known CP violation is far too small to explain it.

mcqs.q: In annihilation of an electron and a positron at rest, the total energy released is
options: 2 m_e c^2, appearing as gamma-ray photons
mcqs.why: Both masses are converted: energy released = (m_e + m_e) c^2 = 2 m_e c^2, carried away by gamma-ray photons.

mcqs.q: The antiproton differs from the proton in having
options: a different lifetime by a large factor
opposite charge (and opposite baryon number), with the same mass
mcqs.why: Proton and antiproton form a pair: same mass and lifetime, opposite charge and opposite values of the other additive quantum numbers.

mcqs.q: Most of the matter and antimatter made in the Big Bang
options: annihilated into radiation, leaving only the small surviving excess of matter we see
is still present in equal amounts
mcqs.why: The rest annihilated into radiation; the surviving excess of about one part in a billion is all the matter we see.

mcqs.q: The known CP violation in weak interactions
options: is far too small to explain the baryon asymmetry, so some early-universe process must have favoured matter
mcqs.why: The notes call the asymmetry an unsolved mystery: known CP violation is far too small, so some process in the very early universe must have favoured matter.

mcqs.q: The neutron's antiparticle is
options: the antineutron, with the same mass but opposite values of the additive quantum numbers
there is none, because the neutron is neutral
mcqs.why: Neutron and antineutron are a pair: neutrality does not prevent an antiparticle — the additive quantum numbers such as baryon number are opposite.

mcqs.q: Annihilation converts mass into
options: a black hole in all cases
mcqs.why: When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate and their mass appears as gamma-ray photons.

lessons.notes_html:

The Strong Nuclear Force

The strong nuclear force is the short-range attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus, overcoming their electrostatic repulsion. It is the strongest of the four forces at its range. Between quarks it is mediated by gluons — massless particles that themselves carry colour charge and bind quarks inside protons, neutrons and other hadrons. The force felt between nucleons is a residual effect of this gluon exchange, carried between nucleons by pions.

Electroweak Unification

At very high energies the electromagnetic and weak forces are two aspects of a single electroweak interaction, mediated by one set of bosons (photon, W+, W- and Z). At ordinary energies the symmetry is broken by the Higgs mechanism, so the forces appear different: electromagnetism is long-ranged, the weak force very short-ranged.

options: the strong nuclear force, with relative strength 1 at its range
mcqs.why: Relative strengths: strong 1, electromagnetic 10^-2, weak 10^-13, gravitational 10^-38 — the strong force is the strongest at its range.

mcqs.why: Between quarks the strong force is mediated by gluons; the force felt between nucleons is a residual effect of gluon exchange, carried between nucleons by pions.

mcqs.why: Electromagnetic: carrier photon, infinite range, relative strength 10^-2 — the second strongest of the four interactions.

mcqs.q: The weak nuclear force is carried by
options: the W+, W- and Z bosons, with range about 10^-18 m and relative strength 10^-13
mcqs.why: Weak nuclear: carriers W+, W- and Z bosons, range about 10^-18 m, relative strength 10^-13.

the strong force at long range
mcqs.why: Gravitational: infinite range but relative strength only 10^-38; its carrier, the graviton, is hypothetical.

mcqs.q: The strong force holds the nucleus together by
options: attracting protons and neutrons to each other, overcoming their electrostatic repulsion
pushing neutrons between the protons as a shield only
mcqs.why: The strong nuclear force is the short-range attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus, overcoming their electrostatic repulsion.

mcqs.q: Electroweak unification says that at very high energies,
options: all four forces including gravity are unified in a proven theory
the electromagnetic and weak forces are two aspects of a single electroweak interaction, mediated by one set of bosons (photon, W+, W-, Z)
the weak force becomes long-ranged at ordinary energies
mcqs.why: At very high energies the two are one electroweak interaction; at ordinary energies the symmetry is broken by the Higgs mechanism, so the forces appear different.

mcqs.q: The force felt between nucleons (protons and neutrons) is a residual effect of gluon exchange, carried between nucleons by
mcqs.why: Gluons bind quarks inside hadrons; the residual strong force between nucleons is carried between them by pions.

mcqs.q: The symmetry between the electromagnetic and weak forces at ordinary energies is broken by
options: the Higgs mechanism, so electromagnetism is long-ranged and the weak force very short-ranged
mcqs.why: The Higgs mechanism breaks the electroweak symmetry at ordinary energies: electromagnetism stays long-ranged while the weak force is very short-ranged.

lessons.title: Quarks, Leptons, Fermions and Bosons
lessons.notes_html:
Quarks

There are six types (flavours) of quark in three generations: (up, down), (charm, strange) and (top, bottom). Ordinary matter is built only from up and down quarks; the heavier flavours appear in high-energy collisions and decay quickly.

  • Baryons are formed by a combination of three quarks (proton = uud, neutron = udd).
  • Mesons are formed by a quark and an antiquark.
  • A neutron is converted into a proton when it absorbs a π+ or emits a π- — the charge balances in both cases.

Strange Particles

Strange particles contain a strange quark. They are produced in pairs by the strong interaction (associated production) but decay slowly by the weak interaction — a puzzling combination that earned them their name and led to the strangeness quantum number. Examples: the K-mesons (kaons) and the lambda hyperon.

Leptons

There are six leptons in three generations: the electron, muon and tau, with their three neutrinos (electron, muon and tau neutrinos). Leptons do not feel the strong force; charged leptons feel the electromagnetic and weak forces, while neutrinos feel only the weak force and gravity.

Fermions and Bosons

  • Fermions: half-integral spin (1/2, 3/2, ...). They obey the Pauli exclusion principle — no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state. Quarks and leptons are fermions; electrons, protons and neutrons are fermions.
  • Bosons: zero or integral spin (0, 1, 2, ...). They do not obey the exclusion principle and can share states. Photons, gluons and the Higgs boson are bosons — the force carriers.

mcqs.q: There are six types (flavours) of quark, in three generations:
mcqs.why: Six quark flavours in three generations: (up, down), (charm, strange), (top, bottom). Ordinary matter is built only from up and down quarks.

mcqs.q: Baryons are formed by
options: a combination of three quarks: proton = uud, neutron = udd
mcqs.why: Baryons are three-quark combinations: the proton is uud and the neutron is udd. Mesons are a quark and an antiquark.

mcqs.q: Mesons are formed by
mcqs.why: Mesons are quark-antiquark pairs, in contrast to baryons, which contain three quarks.

mcqs.q: The quark content of a neutron is
mcqs.why: Neutron = udd (one up, two down quarks), giving total charge 2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0; the proton uud has charge +1.

mcqs.q: There are six leptons in three generations:
options: the electron, muon and tau, with their three neutrinos
mcqs.why: Leptons: electron, muon, tau and the electron, muon and tau neutrinos. Leptons do not feel the strong force.

mcqs.q: Neutrinos feel
options: only the weak force and gravity
mcqs.why: Charged leptons feel the electromagnetic and weak forces, while neutrinos feel only the weak force and gravity — which is why they are so hard to detect.

mcqs.q: Fermions are particles with
options: integral spin that can share states
half-integral spin (1/2, 3/2, ...) that obey the Pauli exclusion principle
mcqs.why: Fermions: half-integral spin, obeying Pauli's principle — no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state. Quarks and leptons are fermions.

mcqs.q: Bosons are particles with
options: only zero mass in all cases
zero or integral spin (0, 1, 2, ...) that do not obey the exclusion principle and can share states; they are the force carriers
mcqs.why: Photons, gluons and the Higgs boson are bosons — the force carriers; they can share quantum states, unlike fermions.

mcqs.q: Strange particles earned their name because they
options: are produced in pairs by the strong interaction (associated production) but decay slowly by the weak interaction — a puzzling combination
have strange colours visible in detectors
were found only in cosmic rays
mcqs.why: Strange particles contain a strange quark; produced strongly in pairs yet decaying slowly (weakly), they led to the strangeness quantum number. Examples: kaons and the lambda hyperon.

mcqs.q: A neutron is converted into a proton when it
options: absorbs a pi+ or emits a pi-, the charge balancing in both cases
mcqs.why: The notes give this pion-exchange picture: absorbing a pi+ (charge +1) or emitting a pi- (charge -1) turns a neutron (0) into a proton (+1) with charge conserved.

lessons.title: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiations
lessons.notes_html:
RadiationNatureMassChargeStopped By
Alpha (α)Helium nuclei (2 protons + 2 neutrons)about 4 u+2ea sheet of paper
Beta (β)Electrons (β-) or positrons (β+)negligible-e or +ea few mm of aluminium
Gamma (γ)High-energy photonszero rest masszerothick lead or concrete

Alpha radiation is heavily ionizing; gamma radiation is the most penetrating. Gamma rays are emitted with discrete energies when a nucleus drops from an excited state.

Why Alpha Energies Are Discrete but Beta Energies Continuous

  • Alpha decay is a two-body decay between two definite nuclear energy levels: the energy is shared by only the alpha particle and the recoiling daughter nucleus, so every alpha particle from that decay carries nearly the same, discrete energy.
  • Beta decay is a three-body decay: the energy is shared among the daughter nucleus, the electron and an antineutrino, so the electron takes a continuous range of energies up to a maximum — the missing energy carried away by the antineutrino, as Pauli proposed to save energy conservation.

Beta-Minus Decay in Detail

In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton (a proton changing into a neutron is beta-plus decay):

n → p + e- + anti-νe

  • At the quark level, a down quark changes into an up quark by emitting a W- boson, which decays into the electron and the antineutrino.
  • Charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved.

Conservation Laws in Reactions and Decays

Every particle reaction or decay must conserve: energy (including mass-energy), linear momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, baryon number, lepton number for each generation, and colour charge. Strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic processes but not in weak decays. A proposed reaction is possible only if it satisfies all of these laws.

options: helium nuclei (2 protons + 2 neutrons), mass about 4 u, charge +2e, stopped by a sheet of paper
mcqs.why: Alpha: helium nuclei, about 4 u, charge +2e, stopped by a sheet of paper; alpha radiation is heavily ionizing.

mcqs.q: Beta radiation consists of
options: electrons (beta-) or positrons (beta+), of negligible mass, stopped by a few mm of aluminium
mcqs.why: Beta particles are fast electrons or positrons with negligible mass and charge -e or +e, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

mcqs.q: Gamma radiation consists of
options: high-energy photons, with zero rest mass and zero charge, stopped only by thick lead or concrete
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are high-energy photons, the most penetrating radiation, emitted with discrete energies when a nucleus drops from an excited state.

mcqs.q: The most penetrating of the three radiations is
mcqs.why: Alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few mm of aluminium, but gamma needs thick lead or concrete: gamma is the most penetrating, while alpha is the most ionizing.

mcqs.q: Alpha particle energies are discrete because alpha decay is
options: a three-body decay with a neutrino
a two-body decay between two definite nuclear energy levels, so the energy is shared by only the alpha particle and the recoiling daughter nucleus
always accompanied by gamma rays of random energy
mcqs.why: With only two bodies sharing a definite energy release, every alpha from that decay carries nearly the same, discrete energy.

mcqs.q: Beta particle energies are continuous because beta decay is
options: a three-body decay: the energy is shared among the daughter nucleus, the electron and an antineutrino, so the electron takes a continuous range up to a maximum
mcqs.why: The antineutrino carries away a variable share — the 'missing energy' Pauli proposed to save energy conservation — so electron energies are continuous up to a maximum.

mcqs.q: In beta-minus decay, a neutron changes into a proton as
options: a proton changes into a neutron
an up quark changes into a down quark
n -> p + e- + anti-neutrino: a down quark changes into an up quark by emitting a W- boson
mcqs.why: Beta-minus: n -> p + e- + anti-nu_e. At quark level a down quark becomes an up quark by emitting a W-, which decays into the electron and antineutrino. Charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved.

mcqs.q: Beta-plus decay is the process in which
options: a proton changes into a neutron
a neutron changes into a proton
an electron is captured by a photon
a nucleus emits a helium nucleus
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two: in beta-minus a neutron becomes a proton; a proton changing into a neutron is beta-plus decay.

mcqs.q: Every particle reaction or decay must conserve
options: energy (including mass-energy), linear momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, baryon number, lepton number for each generation, and colour charge
strangeness in all processes including weak decays
mcqs.why: A proposed reaction is possible only if it satisfies all these conservation laws; strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic processes but not in weak decays.

mcqs.q: Strangeness is NOT conserved in
options: weak decays (it is conserved in strong and electromagnetic processes)
mcqs.why: Strangeness is conserved in strong and electromagnetic processes but not in weak decays — which is why strange particles decay slowly, by the weak interaction.

lessons.title: The Higgs Boson, Plasma and String Theory
lessons.notes_html:
The Higgs Boson and Mass

The Higgs boson is the quantum of the Higgs field, which fills all space, and it is the particle responsible for the mass of the elementary particles. Particles gain mass by interacting with this field: those that interact strongly (like the top quark) are heavy, those that interact weakly (like the electron) are light, and those that do not interact at all (like the photon) stay massless. The Higgs boson itself — the observable excitation of the field, discovered at CERN in 2012 — confirms the mechanism, which also gives mass to the W and Z bosons.

Most Matter in the Universe Is Plasma

Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is an ionized gas of free electrons and ions. Stars are balls of plasma, and the space between stars and galaxies is filled with extremely dilute plasma; the early universe was plasma too. By mass, the solid, liquid and gaseous matter on planets is only a tiny fraction of the universe's ordinary matter — the overwhelming bulk exists as plasma in stars and interstellar space.

String Theory

String theory proposes that the fundamental objects are tiny one-dimensional strings rather than point particles. In its consistent form it requires 10 dimensions of space-time — far more than the four we experience.

Key Points

  • Motion is relative to a frame of reference; Newton's laws hold simply only in inertial frames.
  • Relativity: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for all inertial observers.
  • Moving lengths contract, moving clocks run slow, moving masses increase; E = m c2.
  • Only a particle of zero rest mass can travel at the speed of light.
  • First antiparticle found: the positron (antielectron), 1932.
  • Four interactions: strong (gluons), electromagnetic (photon), weak (W and Z bosons), gravitational (weakest).
  • Six quarks and six leptons, in three generations; baryons are three quarks, mesons a quark and an antiquark.
  • Fermions have half-integral spin and obey Pauli's principle; bosons have integral spin and carry the forces.
  • Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton; alpha energies are discrete, beta energies continuous.
  • The Higgs boson gives elementary particles their mass; most matter in the universe is plasma.
